e_schedule.tip: Same time, same conditions — morning after waking, before eating
e_schedule.keyFact: Weight can fluctuate 1–2 kg daily due to water, gut contents, and menstrual cycle — not actual fat. Only trends over 4–8 weeks are meaningful. Weighing 1–3×/week (not daily) avoids unnecessary anxiety while still capturing trends.
e_schedule.detail: Weigh in the morning after using the bathroom, before breakfast, without heavy clothing — this is when the body is in its most consistent baseline state. Record the number and take a weekly average to eliminate daily noise.
details: Why not daily weighing: daily fluctuations come from sodium (salt retains water), carbohydrates (glycogen holds 3g water/g), menstrual cycle, breathing, sweating. Reacting to a daily number is the source of unnecessary anxiety and poor food decisions.
Optimal frequency: 1–3×/week, same days (e.g. Mon/Wed/Fri morning). Average of 3 = weekly weight. Compare this week to last, not today to yesterday.
Standard conditions each time: after using the toilet (urination), before drinking water or eating breakfast, same device, same flat hard floor. No shoes, no heavy clothing.
Understanding trends: loss >0.25 kg/week for 4 consecutive weeks = true downward trend. Fluctuations within ±1 kg vs last week = no change. Gain >0.5 kg/week for 3–4 weeks = review diet.

When not to weigh: after a large meal, after a heavy workout (muscles retain water for recovery), just before/after menstrual cycle, when ill with fever. At these times the number does not reflect reality.

Useful tracking apps: Happy Scale (iOS) or LibreScale (Android) compute a moving average and remove noise — showing the true trend when daily numbers look chaotic. Or use a simple spreadsheet: date, weight, 7-day average.

points.label: 1–3×/week is enough
points.note: More creates anxiety — no added useful information

points.label: Morning, after bathroom, before eating
points.note: Most consistent baseline of the day

points.label: Look at the weekly average
points.note: Removes daily noise — 4-week trend is what matters

points.label: Don't react to a single number
points.note: ±1–2 kg fluctuation is normal physiology, not fat

e_schedule.tip: More important than weight — reflects visceral fat risk
e_schedule.keyFact: Waist circumference reflects visceral fat — more dangerous than body weight alone. Danger thresholds for Asians: ≥90 cm for men, ≥80 cm for women (IDF Asia standard). Just a tape measure and 30 seconds — this is the most important cardiovascular metric you can self-measure at home.
e_schedule.detail: Visceral fat (around abdominal organs) acts differently from subcutaneous fat: it secretes inflammatory adipokines and free fatty acids directly into the portal circulation, causing insulin resistance and atherosclerosis. A 5–10 cm waist reduction is linked to significant cardiovascular and diabetes risk reduction, even when weight changes little.
details: How to measure correctly: stand straight, feet shoulder-width apart, exhale gently (do NOT suck in or exhale fully), measure at the midpoint between the bottom of the last rib and the top of the iliac crest — usually level with or 1–2 cm above the navel. Do not pull the tape too tight or leave it loose. Measure twice, take the average.

Once a week is optimal: waist changes more slowly than weight (this is actual fat, not water). Daily measuring shows no change and discourages. Trends become clear over 4–8 weeks. Same morning before eating, same conditions.

Understanding Asian thresholds: IDF 2005 set lower thresholds than Western standards because Asians accumulate more visceral fat at the same BMI. Men ≥90 cm (Western 102 cm), women ≥80 cm (Western 88 cm). Normal BMI but waist above threshold = TOFI — metabolic risk equivalent to overweight.

Waist shrinks before weight: when starting a healthy diet and exercise, visceral fat (reflected in waist) often decreases before the scale moves significantly. Waist down 2–3 cm while weight unchanged = true success — losing fat and gaining muscle.

Non-dietary factors affecting waist: chronic stress (cortisol drives abdominal fat accumulation), poor sleep (<6h causes high cortisol), alcohol (especially beer belly), long-term corticosteroids. Reducing waist requires addressing all these factors, not just eating less.

When to be concerned: waist increases >3 cm in 1 month without explanation, or increases with facial/leg swelling, unusual fatigue, shortness of breath → medical evaluation needed (rule out ascites, heart failure, kidney failure).

points.label: Men <90 cm · Women <80 cm
points.note: IDF Asia threshold — lower than Western due to different physiology

points.label: Measure correctly: gentle exhale, no sucking in
points.note: Sucking in or full exhale skews results by 3–5 cm

points.label: Waist shrinks before weight
points.note: Visceral fat responds quickly — earliest sign of progress

points.label: TOFI: normal BMI but high waist
points.note: Metabolic risk despite normal weight — waist measurement is mandatory

e_schedule.tip: 5 min sitting rest before measuring — both arms
e_schedule.keyFact: Hypertension is called the 'silent killer' because it has no clear symptoms until complications arise (stroke, heart attack, kidney failure). Seven-day home monitoring averages (morning + evening) are more accurate than a single clinic reading because they eliminate white-coat hypertension (BP elevated by anxiety at the doctor).
e_schedule.detail: Blood pressure changes continuously throughout the day: lowest during sleep, rising from 6–10 am (morning surge), highest in late afternoon. A single reading can be 10–20 mmHg off from the true value. Standard protocol: measure twice, 1–2 minutes apart, average both, record both morning and evening.
details: Correct preparation before measuring: sit quietly for 5 minutes (no talking, no phone). No coffee, no smoking, no exercise in the 30 minutes before. Empty bladder (full bladder raises BP 10–15 mmHg). Sit up straight, feet flat on the floor, do not cross legs.

Cuff position: arm at heart level (on a table, at chest height). Cuff should cover 80% of arm circumference (wrong size causes ±10 mmHg error). Do not measure over thick clothing. Rest at least 1 minute between readings, average both.

Measurement frequency by situation: healthy individuals — 2–3×/week is enough to detect trends. Those with diagnosed or suspected high BP — measure morning + evening daily for 7 days, record, bring results to doctor. Those adjusting medication — follow doctor's guidance.

Reading numbers correctly: 120/80 = systolic/diastolic. Normal: <120/80. Elevated: 120–129/<80. Stage 1 HTN: 130–139/80–89. Stage 2 HTN: ≥140/90. Hypertensive crisis: >180/>120 → seek care immediately. One high reading is not a diagnosis — multiple readings on different occasions are needed.

Masked and white-coat hypertension: normal BP at home but high at clinic = white-coat (25–30% of patients). High BP at home but normal at clinic = masked hypertension (more dangerous because it goes undetected). This is why home monitoring matters as much as clinic readings.

When to seek immediate care: BP ≥180/120 mmHg (even without symptoms), elevated BP with severe headache at back of head, blurred vision, chest pain, shortness of breath, sudden facial/hand/foot swelling, or diastolic BP suddenly >20 mmHg above your baseline.

points.label: Rest 5 minutes before measuring
points.note: Standing, talking, or using phone raises BP by 5–15 mmHg

points.label: Record both readings, both sessions
points.note: 7-day morning + evening average is more accurate than one clinic visit

points.label: Target: <120/80 mmHg
points.note: Stage 1 HTN: 130–139/80–89 → lifestyle changes needed

points.label: ≥180/120 → seek care immediately
points.note: Hypertensive crisis — do not wait even without symptoms

e_schedule.tip: Count 60s after waking — trend over 4 weeks matters
e_schedule.keyFact: Resting heart rate (RHR) is a simple metric reflecting cardiovascular health and recovery level. Regular exercisers have RHR 45–55 bpm; sedentary individuals 75–90 bpm. Research: every 10 bpm increase in RHR is associated with 15–18% higher cardiovascular mortality risk. A sudden RHR spike (>10 bpm above baseline) is an early sign of illness, stress, poor sleep, or overtraining.
e_schedule.detail: RHR must be measured immediately after waking, before sitting up or doing anything — this is the true resting state. Sitting up raises RHR 10–15 bpm, coffee raises it 5–10 bpm, stress raises it 5–20 bpm. Tracking your personal baseline matters more than comparing to generic normal ranges.
details: How to measure accurately: immediately upon waking (eyes just open), still lying still, place 2 fingers (index + middle) on the inner wrist (radial pulse) or neck (carotid), count for 60 seconds. Or 30 seconds × 2. A smartwatch measures continuously and averages overnight — more accurate than a single manual reading.

Normal ranges and their meaning: 60–100 bpm is normal per AHA, but the optimal range for health is 60–80 bpm. Athletes: 40–60 bpm (stronger heart pumping more blood per beat). RHR >100 bpm consistently = tachycardia, needs medical evaluation.

RHR as a recovery barometer: RHR 5–7 bpm above baseline after training = insufficient recovery — train light or rest that day. RHR 7–10+ bpm elevated with fatigue = possible illness coming (viral infection commonly raises RHR before symptoms appear). Garmin/Apple Watch HRV and Recovery Score are based on this.

Improving RHR through training: Zone 2 cardio (running or cycling at a pace where you can still hold a conversation) for 150 min/week is the most effective way to lower RHR long-term. After 8–12 weeks of consistent training, RHR can drop 5–10 bpm. Resistance training also helps but less than cardio.

Factors that raise RHR: dehydration (RHR rises 7–8 bpm with 1% body weight fluid loss), caffeine, stress, sleep deprivation, alcohol (spikes during that night), medications (check instructions). These fluctuations are normal if RHR returns to baseline after 1–2 days.

HRV — a more advanced metric: Heart Rate Variability (variation between heartbeats) reflects autonomic nervous system balance better than RHR alone. High HRV = good recovery, healthy heart. Modern smartwatches measure HRV each morning — if HRV drops more than 20% below your baseline for multiple consecutive days, this signals your body needs rest.

points.label: Measure on waking, before sitting up
points.note: Sitting up immediately adds 10–15 bpm — baseline value is lost

points.label: +5–7 bpm above baseline = under-recovered
points.note: Train light or rest — especially if accompanied by fatigue

points.label: Zone 2 cardio lowers RHR
points.note: 150 min/week → RHR drops 5–10 bpm after 8–12 weeks

points.label: Dehydration raises RHR by 7–8 bpm
points.note: Drink water upon waking before the next measurement

e_schedule.tip: Sleep score + wake count + morning energy (1–10)
e_schedule.keyFact: Sleep affects nearly every organ system. Chronic sleep deprivation (<7 hours/night) is linked to 89% higher obesity risk (in children), type 2 diabetes, hypertension, depression, cognitive decline, and early death. Matthew Walker (Why We Sleep): 'There is no organ in the body that does not benefit from sleep, and no disease that does not worsen with sleep deprivation.'
e_schedule.detail: Tracking sleep daily helps you recognize patterns: do you sleep better after exercise? After eating dinner early? Does it correlate with next-day mood? Personalized data drives improvement more effectively than any generic advice.
details: What to record: bedtime, estimated time to fall asleep, number of night wakings, wake-up time, how you feel on waking (scale 1–5: 1=very tired, 5=refreshed). Total sleep duration + quality (feeling on waking) = the two most important metrics.

Tracking tools: smartwatches (Apple Watch, Garmin, Fitbit) automatically track sleep stages (light/deep/REM). Apps like Sleep Cycle or Oura Ring analyze quality. Minimalist approach: a sleep journal with 3 metrics (bedtime, wake time, quality score 1–5) takes 10 seconds each morning.

Circadian rhythm: the body has a 24-hour internal clock controlling melatonin, cortisol, and body temperature. Going to bed and waking at the same time every day (including weekends) is the single most important factor for sleep quality — more important than the specific bedtime. A >1-hour difference between weekday and weekend schedules (social jet lag) raises obesity and cardiovascular risk.

Deep sleep and REM: deep sleep (N3) is critical for physical recovery, immunity, and growth hormone release. REM is critical for emotional memory, creativity, and stress processing. Deep sleep is concentrated in the first third of the night; REM in the final third. Alcohol suppresses REM strongly — sleeping 8 hours after drinking but missing REM = no real recovery.

Common sleep disruptors: screens before bed (blue light suppresses melatonin for 2–3 hours), room too warm (ideal 18–20°C), caffeine after 2 pm (half-life 5–6h — 25% remains in blood at midnight), drinking a lot of water in the evening, catching up on sleep at weekends.

When tracking reveals patterns: consistently <6h/night for >1 week → prioritize sleep above all other health goals. Quality ≤2/5 despite adequate hours → consider sleep apnea (especially if snoring, high BMI, thick neck). Frequent 2–3 am wakings → high cortisol/stress/anxiety that needs addressing.

points.label: Same sleep/wake time all week
points.note: Stable circadian rhythm matters more than the specific hour

points.label: No screens 1h before bed
points.note: Blue light suppresses melatonin for 2–3 hours — delays sleep onset

points.label: Room at 18–20°C for deep sleep
points.note: Core temperature drops during deep sleep — a cool room supports this

points.label: Alcohol disrupts REM even with enough hours
points.note: 8h sleep after alcohol = missing restorative sleep

e_schedule.tip: Scale 1–10 — notice what days stress spikes
e_schedule.keyFact: Chronic stress (lasting weeks/months) has real physiological effects: persistently high cortisol raises blood pressure, suppresses the immune system, causes insulin resistance, accumulates abdominal fat, and shrinks the hippocampus (brain region critical for memory). Tracking daily stress helps you recognize triggers, patterns, and the effectiveness of interventions (meditation, exercise, sleep).
e_schedule.detail: A simple 1–10 subjective scale is effective when tracked consistently. Absolute score matters less than trends: stress at 6/10 every day for 2 weeks is more dangerous than stress at 8/10 for a single day. Record in the evening before sleep — this time reflects the full day.
details: How to use the 1–10 scale: 1–3 = relaxed, no significant pressure. 4–5 = mild normal stress, manageable. 6–7 = significant stress, affecting focus and mood. 8–9 = very stressed, hard to control. 10 = extreme, crisis. Optionally note 1 word about the main cause (work, family, health, finances).

Common patterns when tracking: high stress every Monday (anticipatory stress), lower stress after exercise (endorphin effect visible in data), stress increases correlating with 2 consecutive nights of poor sleep, stress decreases after >4 weeks of consistent meditation. This personalized data outperforms any generic advice.

Physiological vs perceived stress: HRV (heart rate variability) is a physiological metric reflecting autonomic stress — low = high stress even if you feel fine. Combining HRV from a smartwatch with a subjective stress scale gives a fuller picture. Many people do not feel stressed but have consistently low HRV = high allostatic load.

Most evidence-based interventions: (1) 30-minute moderate exercise — lowers cortisol, raises BDNF and endorphins. (2) 4–7–8 or box breathing — activates the parasympathetic system immediately. (3) Mindfulness meditation >8 weeks — reduces amygdala size, increases prefrontal cortex grey matter (meta-analysis Holzel 2011). (4) Adequate sleep — nighttime cortisol drops during deep sleep.

Allostatic load — total long-term stress burden: the body can handle short bursts of acute stress (actually beneficial). The problem is unrelenting stress without recovery. Track your 7-day average: if consistently ≥6/10 for >2 weeks → active intervention is needed, not just trying harder.

Social connection — often overlooked: loneliness and social isolation have a health impact equivalent to smoking 15 cigarettes a day (Holt-Lunstad 2015). Track social connection alongside stress — often high stress stems from loneliness, not workload. One genuine conversation with a loved one lowers cortisol effectively.

e_schedule.keyFact: The 10,000 steps/day figure comes from a 1965 Japanese marketing campaign, not scientific research. JAMA 2019 study (>16,000 women): benefit starts at 4,400 steps/day and increases up to ~7,500 steps/day — then plateaus. 7,000–8,000 steps is a realistic, evidence-based target for most adults.
e_schedule.detail: Step count is a proxy for NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis) — calories burned through daily activity outside structured exercise. NEAT can vary by up to 2,000 kcal/day between active and sedentary individuals. Increasing daily steps is easier to sustain than gym attendance and can have a larger total weekly calorie impact.
details: Evidence on optimal thresholds: JAMA Internal Medicine 2021 (2,110 middle-aged adults): 7,000+ steps/day reduced cardiovascular mortality risk by 50–70% vs <5,000 steps. Beyond 10,000 steps, additional benefit is minimal. Lancet 2022: optimal threshold is 6,000–8,000 for adults >60, and 8,000–10,000 for younger adults.

Steps vs structured exercise: 10,000 steps/day ≈ 5–7 km walking ≈ 300–400 kcal. Combining high steps (NEAT) + structured exercise (gym/cardio) is better than gym alone while sitting the rest of the day (the active couch potato effect — research confirms 60 min/day of exercise does not offset 8–12h of continuous sitting).

How to add steps without trying: take stairs instead of the elevator, get off the bus 1–2 stops early, walk while on phone calls, use walking meetings, park farther away. These small changes accumulate 2,000–3,000 extra steps/day without extra time.

Intensity matters too: 100 steps/minute = normal walking pace. 130+ steps/minute = brisk walk (light cardio). A continuous 10-minute brisk walking bout provides additional cardiovascular benefits beyond total step count. WHO recommends 150 min moderate activity/week = ~10 min brisk walk × 5 days/week.

Tracking tools: your phone (built-in accelerometer, use Health/Google Fit) is accurate enough for everyday tracking — about 5–10% error. A smartwatch is more accurate. A simple pedometer ($5–10) also works. Key: consistency with one tool matters more than absolute accuracy.

Warning thresholds: <3,000 steps/day consistently for many weeks = sedentary lifestyle with clear health risks. If your job requires prolonged sitting (>6h/day), adding a 5-minute walk every hour (40 min total) reduces cardiovascular risk as much as adding 1,000 steps/day.

signs: Severe crushing chest pain radiating to left arm, jaw, or back
Palpitations with dizziness, chest pain, or difficulty breathing
Very high blood pressure with chest pain, weakness, or confusion
e_emergency.keyFact: Heart attack (MI) and acute heart failure are the two most common cardiovascular emergencies. With MI: each minute without reperfusion ≈ 2 million heart muscle cells die. "Time is muscle" — time from symptom onset to vessel opening (door-to-balloon <90 min) directly determines permanent heart damage and mortality.
e_emergency.detail: Cardiac chest pain is typically described as "crushing," "squeezing," or "a heavy weight on the chest" — not necessarily sharp. 25–30% of MIs are atypical (especially in women, diabetics): only fatigue, nausea, shortness of breath, or jaw/neck pain. Do not wait and see — call 115 immediately.
details: Recognizing MI: crushing chest pain lasting >20 min radiating to the left shoulder, arm (or both), jaw, or mid-back. With cold sweats, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or sense of impending doom. Does not ease with rest or nitroglycerin. Women often present atypically: extreme fatigue, nausea, or shortness of breath only.

Recognizing acute heart failure: sudden severe shortness of breath — especially when lying down (must sit upright to breathe), pink frothy sputum, rapid leg swelling, rapid abdominal distension, distended neck veins. Often triggered by acute MI, severe arrhythmia, or decompensated chronic heart failure.

Dangerous arrhythmias: palpitations with dizziness, syncope, or chest pain = potentially life-threatening rhythm (VT, VF, fast AF, complete heart block). Sudden unexplained loss of consciousness in a patient with known heart disease = suspect arrhythmia until proven otherwise.

Correct action when MI is suspected: (1) Call 115 immediately — do not self-drive. (2) Chew (do not swallow whole) Aspirin 300 mg if not allergic and available. (3) Lie still, relax, avoid exertion. (4) Unlock the door for the ambulance. (5) If cardiac arrest + loss of consciousness: CPR 30 chest compressions : 2 rescue breaths continuously until help arrives.

Stable vs unstable angina: stable angina = occurs with exertion, resolves within 5–10 min of rest or nitroglycerin — needs follow-up but is NOT an emergency. Unstable angina = new onset, increasing frequency, occurs at rest, does not respond to nitroglycerin → go to ER immediately (may be a forming MI).

Hypertensive crisis: BP >180/>120 with chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, blurred vision, one-sided weakness, or seizures → emergency (end-organ damage). BP >180/>120 alone with no symptoms = hypertensive urgency — needs treatment within hours but is less immediately life-threatening.

points.label: Every minute = 2 million heart cells lost
points.note: Time is muscle — call 115, do not wait, do not self-drive to hospital

points.label: Chew Aspirin 300 mg if available
points.note: Reduces clot formation — do this while waiting for the ambulance

points.label: Women/diabetics: atypical symptoms
points.note: Extreme fatigue, nausea, shortness of breath — chest pain not always present

points.label: Pain at rest + no response to NTG

signs: Sudden one-sided arm or leg weakness
e_emergency.keyFact: Stroke is the 2nd leading cause of death and #1 cause of disability worldwide. Each minute of untreated stroke: 1.9 million brain cells die, 14 billion synapses lost. Treatment window for thrombolysis (tPA): 4.5 hours from symptom onset. Every minute saved = 1.9 million brain cells preserved. Use BE-FAST to recognize it quickly.
e_emergency.detail: BE-FAST (Balance-Eyes-Face-Arm-Speech-Time): Loss of Balance (B) + Vision loss (E) + Facial droop (F) + Arm weakness (A) + Slurred speech (S) → Call 115 immediately (T). Hemorrhagic stroke (ruptured vessel) typically starts with a sudden thunderclap headache — treatment differs from ischemic stroke.
details: Recognize with BE-FAST: Balance (sudden loss of balance, staggering gait), Eyes (sudden blurred or lost vision in one eye or half the visual field), Face (facial droop when smiling — ask patient to smile, one side does not lift), Arm (arm weakness — raise both arms, one drifts down), Speech (slurred, garbled, or failing to understand simple questions), Time (call 115 immediately).

TIA (Transient Ischemic Attack) — do not ignore: stroke symptoms that resolve on their own within <1h (usually <5–15 min). 15% of full strokes occur within 48h after a TIA. This is NOT a sign "all is fine" — go to the ER immediately after a TIA, even if symptoms have resolved.

Hemorrhagic vs ischemic stroke: hemorrhagic (20%): sudden worst-ever headache ("thunderclap"), nausea, vomiting, loss of consciousness. Ischemic (80%): focal neurological deficits (one-sided face, body, speech) often without severe headache. Both require emergency care — do not try to distinguish at home.

Treatment time windows: tPA (thrombolysis): 0–4.5h from onset. Mechanical thrombectomy: 0–24h in selected cases. Treatment in the first hour ("golden hour"): near-complete recovery in 30–50% of patients. Every 30-minute delay = 10% reduction in chance of good outcome.

Modifiable stroke risk factors: hypertension (risk factor #1, accounts for 50% of strokes), atrial fibrillation (5× increased risk), diabetes, smoking, high cholesterol, obesity. Good blood pressure control alone reduces stroke risk by 40%. Aspirin 81 mg/day is not recommended for primary prevention without another indication.

Post-stroke recovery: begin physical therapy within 24–48h (if stable) — neuroplasticity is highest in the first 3–6 months. 30% recover nearly fully, 30% have mild disability, 30% have severe disability. Key determinants: time to treatment + intensity of early rehabilitation.

points.note: Balance · Eyes · Face · Arm · Speech · Time (call 115)

signs: Vomiting blood or passing black tarry stools
Very high blood sugar with drowsiness and deep rapid breathing
Very low blood sugar with sweating, trembling, and drowsiness
e_emergency.keyFact: Digestive and metabolic emergencies are varied and easy to overlook because symptoms can be vague. Upper GI bleeding (vomiting blood/black stools) causes rapid blood loss with 10% mortality if untreated. Severe hypoglycemia (<50 mg/dL) causes irreversible brain damage within 5–10 minutes without correction. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening complication with 1–5% mortality.
e_emergency.detail: Distinguishing emergency abdominal pain from routine pain: emergency when pain is sudden and severe, abdomen is rigid (peritonitis), accompanied by high fever with chills, pain does not ease after 30–60 min or worsens. Abdominal pain with shock (low BP, rapid pulse, cold clammy skin) = absolute emergency.
details: Upper GI bleeding — rapid recognition: vomiting bright red blood (active heavy bleeding) or coffee-ground material (partially digested blood). Black tarry stool with a fetid smell (melena) = blood passed through the gut, source is esophagus/stomach/duodenum. 150–200 mL of blood is enough to cause melena. Causes: peptic ulcer, ruptured esophageal varices (cirrhosis), Mallory-Weiss tear.

Acute hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL with symptoms): trembling, sweating, intense hunger, rapid heartbeat, anxiety — early signs when still conscious and able to self-treat: take 15–20g fast sugar (4 glucose tablets, 150 mL fruit juice, 1 tsp honey), recheck after 15 min. Severe: confusion, seizures, loss of consciousness → inject glucagon (if available) and call 115 immediately.

DKA (Diabetic ketoacidosis): blood sugar >300 mg/dL + nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain + fruity/acetone breath odor + deep rapid breathing (Kussmaul) + drowsiness. Usually in type 1 or type 2 diabetes under stress, infection, or medication non-compliance. Requires IV fluids and insulin urgently at hospital — do not self-treat at home.

Appendicitis — recognition: pain typically starts around the navel then moves to the right lower quadrant, worsens with movement, low-grade fever. If ruptured: pain spreads across abdomen, rigid abdomen, high fever — surgical emergency. Atypical in children, elderly, or pregnant women: pain may be in different location.

Bowel obstruction: cramping intermittent abdominal pain, bloating, nausea/vomiting, no passing gas or stool. Complete obstruction is an emergency — bowel can become ischemic and necrose within hours. Adhesion obstruction (after previous abdominal surgery) is most common in adults.

When abdominal pain needs immediate ER: sudden severe pain (especially "tearing" in back/abdomen → suspect ruptured aortic aneurysm), rigid abdomen on palpation, shock signs (rapid pulse, low BP, cold skin), bloody vomit or black stools, pain not easing after 1–2h or worsening, fever >38.5°C with chills.

signs: Pain after trauma with limb deformity
Back pain with leg weakness, urinary retention, or saddle numbness
Unable to bear weight after injury
e_emergency.keyFact: Musculoskeletal emergencies rarely cause death but can lead to permanent disability if treated late. Cauda equina syndrome (spinal cord tail compression) with leg weakness + urinary retention/incontinence + perineal numbness is a surgical emergency — delay >6–12h can cause permanent loss of bladder/bowel control. Cervical spine fracture after trauma not properly immobilized may cause permanent quadriplegia.
e_emergency.detail: Pain after trauma with limb deformity is almost always a fracture until proven otherwise by X-ray. Do not try to straighten the limb, do not allow the patient to stand or walk. Immobilize with a temporary splint in the current position and transport safely. Note: fractures can cause significant blood loss (femur: 1–2 L, pelvis: 3–5 L).
details: Recognizing fracture: severe pain at the injury site, rapid swelling, obvious deformity (protruding bone, shortened or angulated limb), inability to bear weight, cracking sensation at time of injury. Open fracture (bone penetrating skin) = emergency due to risk of serious infection — requires antibiotics and treatment within 6–8h.

Cauda equina syndrome — surgical emergency: massive lumbar disc herniation compressing the cauda equina causes: low back pain + bilateral leg weakness + saddle numbness (perineum, genitals, inner thighs) + sphincter dysfunction (urinary retention/incontinence, severe constipation or fecal incontinence). Decompression surgery within 24–48h = good prognosis; delay = permanent nerve damage.

Cervical spine fracture after trauma: strong head/neck trauma (motor vehicle accident, horse riding fall, diving head-first) with neck pain = treat as cervical fracture until CT rules it out. Do not freely move the head/neck. Requires a rigid cervical collar and flat board transport. Improper movement = permanent quadriplegia from spinal cord injury.

Compartment syndrome: after fracture/crush/burn — pressure within a fascial compartment rises, cutting off blood supply → severe unexplained pain, pain worsened by passive muscle stretching, tense compartment, distal numbness. Treatment window: 6h — delay causes irreversible muscle necrosis (rhabdomyolysis).

Dislocations — do not reduce at scene: shoulder (most common), hip, knee, elbow dislocations. Severe pain, limb in abnormal position, no movement. Do not reduce at home — fracture may coexist or vascular/nerve damage may be present. Check distal pulse, sensation, and movement. Go to ER for X-ray before reduction.

When back pain needs immediate ER: routine back pain (<6 weeks, no limb weakness, no sphincter dysfunction) is not an emergency. GO TO ER IMMEDIATELY when back pain is accompanied by: rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness, urinary retention or incontinence, saddle numbness (cauda equina), high fever with chills (suspected vertebral osteomyelitis), history of cancer (suspected spinal metastasis), severe trauma.

e7_info_filter.keyFact: 💡 A high follower count ≠ medical expertise. Always verify actual credentials.
e7_info_filter.detail: Anyone sharing health information should have verifiable professional grounding — not just personal experience or high view counts.
details: Licensed doctors, pharmacists, and registered dietitians are credible sources — ask for specific credentials if unsure.
Trusted health organisations: WHO, Ministry of Health, Vietnam Medical Association, Mayo Clinic, and WebMD are reliable sources.
Influencers sharing 'personal journeys' may be inspirational but are not medical advice — clearly distinguish between the two.
Verify by searching the person's name plus 'qualifications', 'professional licence', or check official government websites.
Be cautious with self-proclaimed titles: 'expert' or 'Dr' without a named institution cannot be verified.
A YouTube or TikTok channel with millions of followers does not validate medical accuracy — popularity does not equal truth.

e7_info_filter.tip: Study or personal experience? Sources cited?
e7_info_filter.keyFact: 💡 'I tried it and it worked' is anecdote, not scientific evidence. Controlled studies are needed.
e7_info_filter.detail: Evidence quality determines the reliability of health information — the gap between personal opinion and a clinical trial is vast.
details: Evidence hierarchy (strongest to weakest): systematic review → RCT → cohort study → case report → expert opinion → personal experience.
When reviewing a health claim, look for citations: which journal, how many participants, how long was follow-up.
Animal or in-vitro studies do not automatically apply to humans — clinical trials in humans are needed to confirm findings.
Correlation ≠ causation: 'people who eat X live longer' does not prove X is the cause — there may be confounding factors.
Small samples (n<50), no control group, self-reported outcomes — signs of weak research requiring caution.
Google Scholar and PubMed are free tools anyone can use to verify cited research.

e7_info_filter.keyFact: 💡 Evidence-based medicine never uses absolute language. 'Always effective' and 'no side effects' are warning signs.
e7_info_filter.detail: Health marketing uses emotional language to create false trust — recognising these patterns is an essential self-protection skill.
details: Common red flags: '100% natural', 'no side effects', 'cures completely', 'works for everyone', 'what doctors don't want you to know'.
'Natural' does not mean safe — arsenic and opioids are natural but highly toxic; many synthetic medicines save lives.
Medicine uses probabilistic language: 'may reduce risk', 'supports treatment', 'needs further study' — never absolute.
'Secret cures that pharmaceutical companies are hiding' is a classic conspiracy framing with no factual basis.
Testimonials from a few people cannot replace statistical data from thousands of participants in a study.
When a claim sounds too good to be true — it usually isn't. The 'too good to be true' effect is especially common in health.

e7_info_filter.tip: Fear → expert → solution → sell = manipulation formula.
e7_info_filter.keyFact: 💡 The FASO formula (Fear → Authority → Solution → Offer) is the structure behind thousands of health livestreams. Recognising it helps you avoid manipulation.
e7_info_filter.detail: Genuine health content aims to educate, not to sell immediately. When education and selling are intertwined, question the creator's motivation.
details: FASO formula: Fear (create fear about disease) → Authority (pose as expert) → Solution (introduce remedy) → Offer (sell product) — appears in thousands of livestreams.
'Your liver is being damaged without you knowing… Fortunately there's this product' — a textbook example of the FASO sequence.
Legitimate health education does not require immediate purchase links or flash sales, and does not create time pressure ('only 10 spots left').
Conflict of interest: a supplement seller cannot objectively evaluate that same supplement — financial interest distorts information.
Affiliate links and referral codes do not automatically make information wrong — but know the financial motivation of the sharer.
Simple test: 'Would this person share the information even if I bought nothing?' — helps assess true motivation.

e7_info_filter.tip: 'Stop medication' — extremely dangerous for chronic patients.
e7_info_filter.keyFact: 💡 Abruptly stopping treatment can be life-threatening for heart disease, diabetes, schizophrenia, and epilepsy. Never do this without a doctor's guidance.
e7_info_filter.detail: Advising people to quit conventional medical treatment is the most serious red line — consequences may be irreversible for many chronic conditions.
details: Highest-risk groups when stopping medication abruptly: cardiovascular disease (heart attack, heart failure), diabetes (diabetic coma), epilepsy (continuous seizures), schizophrenia (acute relapse).
'Western medicine has side effects' is true — but not taking medication for serious illness is far more dangerous. Doctors weigh benefit vs. risk for each individual.
No one has the right to advise stopping your medication except your treating physician — this is a clear legal and ethical boundary.
'Complementary treatments' (herbs, acupuncture, psychotherapy) may be used ALONGSIDE medical treatment, not INSTEAD of it — this is called integrative medicine.
If you wish to change your treatment regimen, do it with your doctor: taper gradually, monitor indicators, have a contingency plan — never stop abruptly.
Report to health authorities when encountering content advising treatment cessation: this violates health advertising regulations and may be subject to criminal penalties.

e7_danger_phrases.tip: Abruptly stopping medication can be life-threatening with chronic diseases.
e7_danger_phrases.keyFact: 💡 Stopping blood pressure, cardiac, or diabetes medication abruptly can cause stroke, heart attack, or coma within hours.
e7_danger_phrases.detail: This is the most dangerous advice in the online health world — it sounds natural but can cause irreversible consequences.
details: Medications for chronic conditions (hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, epilepsy) cannot be stopped abruptly — the body has adapted and doses must be tapered under medical guidance.
Abruptly stopping blood pressure medication: risk of rebound hypertension — blood pressure spikes higher than pre-treatment levels, potentially causing stroke within 24–48 hours.
Stopping anti-epileptic drugs: seizure rebound can occur even in patients with good control for many years — status epilepticus is a medical emergency.
Abruptly stopping corticosteroids: acute adrenal insufficiency (Addisonian crisis) — shock, hypotension, life-threatening.
'Western medicines have side effects' is true — but doctors have weighed benefits against risks. To make changes, work with your doctor, do not self-stop.
If you genuinely want to reduce medication: positive lifestyle changes (diet, exercise) can support this — but done ALONGSIDE treatment, not REPLACING it, and under medical supervision.

e7_danger_phrases.tip: The liver does not need 'detoxing' — it is the body's best self-cleaning organ.
e7_danger_phrases.keyFact: 💡 No scientific evidence supports commercial 'liver detox'. The liver is an extraordinarily efficient filtration organ — if real 'detoxification' is needed, you require hospitalisation, not herbal tea.
e7_danger_phrases.detail: The concept of 'liver detox' in medicine means something entirely different from commercial products — this is one of the most widespread health misconceptions.
details: The liver processes 1.5 litres of blood per minute, removing toxins 24/7 — it does not need 'rest' or 'stimulation' from herbal teas or supplements.
In medicine, real 'liver detoxification' is ICU treatment: plasmapheresis, emergency liver transplant for acute liver failure from severe poisoning.
Many commercial 'liver detox' products contain insufficiently researched ingredients — paradoxically, they may cause liver damage themselves (DILI — drug-induced liver injury).
Celery juice, artichoke tea, and silymarin (milk thistle) have limited data — they cannot 'detox' or reverse pre-existing liver damage.
How to truly protect your liver: avoid alcohol, maintain healthy weight, get hepatitis B vaccination, do not self-medicate with high-dose herbs.
If concerned about liver health: test AST, ALT, GGT, bilirubin — real results, no money wasted on unproven products.

e7_danger_phrases.tip: No drug or supplement is suitable for all people.
e7_danger_phrases.keyFact: 💡 Modern medicine is moving towards precision medicine — the same drug may save one person but harm another, depending on genetics, underlying conditions, and drug interactions.
e7_danger_phrases.detail: The claim 'suitable for everyone' violates fundamental pharmacology and medicine principles — each person has a unique physiological profile, underlying conditions, and drug response.
details: The same medication: fast metabolisers (extensive metabolisers) need higher doses than slow metabolisers (poor metabolisers) — due to CYP450 enzyme genetic polymorphisms.
Commonly overlooked contraindications: iron not with haemochromatosis; calcium not ideal for calcium oxalate kidney stone patients; high-dose omega-3 with anticoagulants.
Pregnant women: most 'natural' herbs have no safety data in pregnancy — caution is the default principle.
Children are not miniature adults: doses, formulations, and safety profiles differ entirely — adult products are not automatically safe for children.
Chronic kidney disease (CKD): many supplements accumulate when kidneys lose filtering capacity — potassium, phosphorus, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) need tight control.
Herb-drug interactions: St. John's Wort reduces efficacy of oral contraceptives, anti-rejection drugs, and HIV medications — 'natural' does not mean non-interacting.

e7_danger_phrases.tip: No product can 'clean' blood vessels as commercial advertising implies.
e7_danger_phrases.keyFact: 💡 Atherosclerosis is a chronic process requiring serious medical treatment (statins, lifestyle change). No supplement can 'rinse away' plaque that has already formed.
e7_danger_phrases.detail: The concept of 'cleaning blood vessels' in advertising has no correspondence to any scientifically confirmed physiological mechanism — this is popular cardiovascular pseudoscience.
details: Atherosclerosis is the formation of lipid + inflammatory cell + calcium plaques inside vessel walls — it develops over decades and cannot be 'washed away' by supplements.
Real atherosclerosis treatment: statins (reduce LDL, stabilise plaque), aspirin (anti-platelet), blood pressure control, smoking cessation — all require medical monitoring.
Garlic, omega-3, coenzyme Q10, vitamin E: have some data on supporting cardiovascular health — but none of these 'clean' blood vessels with established plaque.
Assessing vascular health realistically: lipid panel (LDL, HDL, triglycerides), carotid Doppler ultrasound, coronary CT calcium score.
'Unblocking blood vessels' in traditional medicine advertising usually implies improving circulation — entirely different from evidence-based atherosclerosis treatment.
If concerned about cardiovascular health: regular blood pressure checks, lipid panel, blood sugar control, no smoking — these are the evidence-based measures.

points.label: Plaque cannot be 'rinsed'
points.note: Requires specialist medical intervention

points.label: Statins are real treatment
points.note: Strongest evidence for atherosclerosis

points.label: Measure blood lipids
points.note: LDL/HDL/triglycerides — real numbers

points.label: Lifestyle > supplements
points.note: Exercise + diet have higher evidence than pills

e7_safe_phrases.tip: Acknowledges product limits — supports only, does not replace treatment.
e7_safe_phrases.keyFact: 💡 'Supports' in medicine means it supplements the primary treatment, not replaces it. This phrase reflects honesty about the product's role.
e7_safe_phrases.detail: The language 'supports monitoring' accurately reflects the position of many health products — they have a complementary role but are not treatment tools.
details: 'Supports monitoring' acknowledges that the product does not cure disease — this is necessary honesty in health communication.
Valid example: a heart rate monitor supports monitoring — it needs a doctor to interpret results and make treatment decisions.
Clear distinction: 'supports blood glucose monitoring' (a meter) is different from 'treating diabetes' (medication + insulin + lifestyle change).
This language helps users set appropriate expectations — not believing that monitoring alone is sufficient; primary treatment is still needed.
Good monitoring tools (apps, wearables, meters) have real value when used alongside medical care, not as a substitute for it.
When you see this phrase, the next question is: 'What is being monitored? How often? When should results be reported to a doctor?' — to know how to use it correctly.

points.label: Acknowledges limits
points.note: Honest about complementary role

points.label: Alongside primary treatment
points.note: Supplements, does not replace

points.label: Monitoring tools
points.note: Wearables, apps — valuable when used correctly

points.label: Ask specifically
points.note: What to monitor? When to report to doctor?

e7_safe_phrases.tip: Acknowledges no one-size-fits-all solution — reflects real medical practice.
e7_safe_phrases.keyFact: 💡 Precision medicine — the direction of modern medicine — is built on this principle: each person needs an individualised protocol based on genetics, lifestyle, and underlying conditions.
e7_safe_phrases.detail: Personalisation is a core principle of modern medicine — this phrase reflects scientific thinking, not avoiding commitment.
details: Protein needs: 0.8–2.2 g/kg depending on goal (weight loss, muscle gain, kidney disease), age, activity level — no single number fits everyone.
Vitamin D dose: depends on current 25-OH vitamin D level, sun exposure, skin colour, BMI — test first, then supplement.
Exercise plan: someone with knee pain needs different exercises than a healthy person; older adults need to prioritise balance and fall prevention over strength.
Diet: people with IBS need low-FODMAP; diabetics need GI control; kidney failure patients need potassium and phosphorus restriction.
When a product or service says 'needs personalisation', this is a positive signal — they do not overpromise and acknowledge you need individual assessment.
Next step when hearing this phrase: 'Personalised based on what information? Who evaluates? Are tests needed?' — to understand the specific process.

points.label: Precision medicine
points.note: Modern medicine based on genetics + lifestyle

points.label: No overpromising
points.note: Acknowledges no universal solution

points.label: Specific assessment needed
points.note: Tests, history, personal goals

e7_safe_phrases.tip: Correct recommendation — recognises personal limits and redirects to a professional.
e7_safe_phrases.keyFact: 💡 This phrase is not avoiding responsibility — it is the most accurate advice possible when insufficient personal information is known to make a specific recommendation.
e7_safe_phrases.detail: The advice 'consult a doctor' is often seen as avoidance, but it actually demonstrates honesty and responsibility in health communication.
details: A doctor can ask direct questions, review medical history, perform a physical examination, read test results — all things online content cannot do.
Online health content provides general information, not medical advice — these two concepts differ legally and ethically.
In many countries, only licensed physicians may provide personalised 'medical advice' — this regulation protects patients.
When someone says 'consult a doctor', treat it as a sign they understand their own limits — not avoidance but responsibility.
This phrase is especially important for: pregnant women, children, elderly people, those with underlying conditions, those taking multiple medications simultaneously.
How to make good use of it: note what you've read, prepare specific questions for your doctor at the next appointment — online content and doctors complement each other.

points.label: Doctor knows you specifically
points.note: History, medications, test results

points.label: Info ≠ medical advice
points.note: Two legally distinct concepts

points.label: Sign of honesty
points.note: The speaker knows their limits

points.label: Use it wisely
points.note: Write questions → ask doctor next appointment

e7_safe_phrases.tip: Clearly states product role — complementary, not replacing treatment.
e7_safe_phrases.keyFact: 💡 Integrative medicine (combining conventional and complementary therapies) always emphasises: complementary therapies do not replace core treatment.
e7_safe_phrases.detail: This is the most honest and important disclaimer in health communication — the product clearly knows its role in the healthcare ecosystem.
details: A product can complement medical treatment: reduce side effects, improve quality of life, support recovery — but not as a dose replacement.
Example: ginger supports reducing nausea during chemotherapy — has some scientific evidence, but does not replace the oncologist's chemotherapy protocol.
When a product says 'does not replace treatment', this is honesty about its limits — do not see it as a weakness but as a sign of trustworthiness.
Integrative medicine at major hospitals (MD Anderson, Mayo Clinic) uses yoga, meditation, acupuncture — ALONGSIDE cancer treatment, not replacing it.
Danger arises when patients decide to replace treatment with 'natural' alternatives — usually due to misinformation or advertising manipulation.
The right question: 'Does this complementary therapy interact with my treatment medication?' — ask your doctor and pharmacist before adding anything.
