Causes of low HDL: smoking (−4–10 mg/dL), abdominal obesity, physical inactivity, refined carbohydrate excess, type 2 diabetes, high TG, beta-blockers and steroids.

Ways to raise HDL: aerobic exercise 150 min/week (+3–9 mg/dL); quitting smoking (+4–10 mg/dL); weight loss — every 3 kg lost raises HDL ~1 mg/dL; moderate alcohol also raises HDL but other risks outweigh the benefit.

"HDL paradox": potent HDL-raising drugs (CETP inhibitors such as torcetrapib) failed to reduce cardiovascular events in trials despite raising HDL by 70%. HDL's cholesterol-collecting function matters more than its concentration.
HDL > 100 mg/dL is not "the higher the better": gene mutations causing very high HDL may impair its function. The practical ideal range is 60–90 mg/dL.

points.label: Exercise: +3–9 mg/dL HDL
points.note: 150 min aerobic/week — most effective method

points.label: Quit smoking: +4–10 mg/dL
points.note: Improvement visible within 2–4 weeks

points.label: Function > quantity of HDL
points.note: Drug trials failed — exercise does not

points.label: −3 kg → +1 mg/dL HDL
points.note: Sustainable, gradual weight loss

lipid_panel_tr.label: Triglycerides
lipid_panel_tr.desc: Blood fats. Elevated by refined carbs, sugar, alcohol, and lack of exercise.
lipid_panel_tr.keyFact: 💡 TG ≥ 500 mg/dL is a medical emergency — risk of acute pancreatitis spikes sharply. TG is very diet-sensitive: reducing refined sugar + eliminating alcohol can lower TG 30–50% within 4 weeks. High-dose omega-3 (2–4g EPA+DHA/day) reduces TG a further 20–45%.
lipid_panel_tr.detail: Triglycerides are the body's primary energy storage form in fat tissue. Elevated blood TG reflects the body receiving more energy from sugars, starches, and alcohol than it can use — not necessarily from dietary fat.
details: Sources of blood TG: (1) Excess carbs → liver converts them to TG packaged into VLDL; (2) Alcohol → ethanol metabolism is prioritized → TG accumulates; (3) Dietary fat → chylomicrons absorbed from gut. Post-meal TG rises sharply — a 9–12h fast is needed for an accurate reading.

High TG and low HDL often coexist: VLDL exchanges lipids with HDL → HDL loses lipid, shrinks, and is rapidly cleared by the kidneys → HDL falls. This is the typical "metabolic syndrome" lipid pattern in sedentary, high-sugar dieters.

TG-induced acute pancreatitis: when TG > 500 mg/dL, pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes TG in pancreatic capillaries → free fatty acids become toxic → pancreatitis. TG > 1000 mg/dL carries very high risk. Treatment: IV insulin + fasting + fibrates.

Secondary causes to rule out: poorly controlled diabetes, hypothyroidism, kidney failure, medications (corticosteroids, retinoids, beta-blockers, tamoxifen). Treating the cause usually improves TG significantly.
Most effective lifestyle changes: reduce simple sugars + refined carbs; eliminate alcohol entirely; high-dose omega-3 (2–4g EPA+DHA/day) lowers TG 20–45%; aerobic exercise; weight loss.
Fibrates (fenofibrate, gemfibrozil) reduce TG 30–50% and raise HDL 10–20% — indicated when TG > 500 mg/dL to prevent pancreatitis, or > 200 mg/dL in high-CV-risk patients already on statins.

points.label: Cut sugar and refined carbs
points.note: Leading cause of high TG in young adults

points.label: Omega-3 cuts TG 20–45%
points.note: 2–4g EPA+DHA/day — equivalent to medication

points.label: Eliminate alcohol
points.note: TG is highly sensitive to alcohol — drops fast when stopped

points.label: TG ≥ 500: pancreatitis risk
points.note: Urgent drug treatment required

rf_groups_tr.title: Stroke — Call 115 Immediately
rf_groups_tr.action: Call 115 or go to ER immediately — every minute 1.9 million brain cells die in stroke.
rf_groups_tr.keyFact: ⏱️ "Time is Brain": every minute of delayed treatment = 1.9 million neurons die. In the first 4.5 hours, clot-dissolving medication (tPA) can reverse damage. Recognize FAST and call emergency services — that is the only thing you need to do.
details: FAST rule: F (Face drooping), A (Arm weakness — cannot raise both arms), S (Speech difficulty — slurred, nonsensical), T (Time — call emergency services immediately when ≥ 1 sign is present).
Ischemic stroke (85%): arterial blockage in the brain. Treatment: tPA thrombolysis within 4.5h, or mechanical thrombectomy within 6–24h at a stroke center.
Hemorrhagic stroke (15%): ruptured blood vessel in the brain. Do NOT give aspirin — it can worsen bleeding. Requires surgery or endovascular intervention.
TIA ("mini stroke"): stroke-like symptoms that resolve within < 24h (usually < 1h). Do not underestimate — 10–15% of TIAs lead to a true stroke within 3 months, highest risk in the first 48h.

What NOT to do: (1) No food or drink — aspiration risk; (2) Do not transport by motorbike — vibration worsens hemorrhage; (3) Do not give blood pressure medication without guidance; (4) Do not wait to see if it resolves on its own.
Prevention: control blood pressure (target < 130/80), no smoking, manage atrial fibrillation (cause of 20% of strokes), statins if LDL is elevated, aspirin only when prescribed by a doctor.

points.label: Golden window: 4.5 hours
points.note: tPA most effective within 3h — call emergency services now

points.label: No aspirin if stroke type unknown
points.note: Hemorrhagic stroke: aspirin makes it worse

points.label: TIA must not be ignored
points.note: 10–15% → true stroke within 3 months

points.label: Do not transport by motorbike
points.note: Vibration can worsen hemorrhagic bleeding

rf_groups_tr.note: Remember the FAST rule — Face drooping · Arm weakness · Speech difficulty · Time to call 115.

rf_groups_tr.title: Heart Attack
rf_groups_tr.action: Call 115 immediately, chew 1 aspirin 300mg (if not allergic), rest — do not drive yourself.
rf_groups_tr.keyFact: 💊 Chew 300mg aspirin immediately (do not swallow whole) if not allergic — it thins the clot blocking the coronary artery. "Door-to-balloon" < 90 minutes is the gold standard: the sooner you arrive at hospital, the more heart muscle is saved.
details: Mechanism: atherosclerotic plaque in the coronary artery ruptures → sudden thrombus forms → complete blockage → heart muscle oxygen deprivation → necrosis. It does not self-resolve — every minute = more dead heart tissue.
Classic symptoms in men: central or left chest pain described as squeezing, crushing, or burning; lasting > 15 minutes; radiating to jaw, neck, left arm, or back; accompanied by sweating, nausea.

Atypical symptoms (common in women, diabetics, elderly): sudden extreme fatigue, unexplained shortness of breath, nausea, dizziness, jaw or back pain — without obvious chest pain. These patients typically arrive later at hospital.

Correct first aid: (1) Call emergency services first; (2) Sit or lie comfortably, loosen clothing; (3) Chew (do not swallow) one 300mg aspirin tablet if not allergic; (4) Nitroglycerin spray under tongue if already prescribed; (5) Nothing to eat or drink; (6) Do not drive yourself.

Hospital treatment: PCI (coronary stenting) within < 90 minutes of arrival is the gold standard. If PCI is unavailable, thrombolysis (tPA) within 30 minutes. Each minute of delay = ~2,000 more heart muscle cells dead.

Recovery after heart attack: cardiac rehabilitation programs reduce recurrence risk by 25–30%. Maintenance drugs: aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor for 1 year, statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor — do not stop without medical advice.

points.label: Aspirin 300mg — chew immediately
points.note: Thins the clot — do not swallow whole

points.label: Do not drive yourself to hospital
points.note: Dangerous if you lose consciousness on the road

points.label: Women: different symptoms from men
points.note: Fatigue, nausea, shortness of breath — not always chest pain

points.label: Door-to-balloon < 90 minutes
points.note: Every minute of delay = more heart muscle death

rf_groups_tr.note: Women may not experience typical chest pain. Symptoms can include jaw pain, nausea, or unusual fatigue. Do not dismiss these signs.

rf_groups_tr.title: Severe Infection / Septic Shock
rf_groups_tr.action: Go to emergency immediately — do not wait to see if medication helps.
rf_groups_tr.keyFact: ⏱️ "Hour-1 Bundle" (sepsis management in the first hour): blood cultures → broad-spectrum antibiotics → fluid resuscitation 30 ml/kg. Mortality increases 7% for every hour of antibiotic delay. Early recognition saves lives.
details: Sepsis: excessive systemic inflammatory response to infection → multi-organ damage. Septic shock: requires vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg + lactate > 2 mmol/L. Mortality 40–50%.
Early warning signs (qSOFA): (1) Respiratory rate > 22/min; (2) Altered mental status (confusion, drowsiness); (3) Systolic BP < 100 mmHg. ≥ 2 criteria → high sepsis risk.

Bacterial meningitis: stiff neck + fever + severe headache + light sensitivity. Do not wait for lumbar puncture before starting antibiotics — each hour of delay increases risk of permanent neurological damage.
Non-blanching purpura (press a finger on the rash — if it does not pale): indicates bloodstream infection (meningococcemia) — maximum emergency.
Common infection sources leading to sepsis: pneumonia (50%), abdominal infection (20%), urinary tract infection (15%), skin/soft tissue infection (10%). Source control must accompany antibiotics.
Prevention: pneumococcal and influenza vaccines; proper wound care; do not self-medicate with antibiotics for persistent fever — masking sepsis symptoms is dangerous.

points.label: +7% mortality per hour of antibiotic delay
points.note: Early antibiotics are the most critical intervention

points.label: Non-blanching rash = maximum emergency
points.note: Meningococcemia — risk of death within hours

points.label: Fluid resuscitation 30 ml/kg in first 3h
points.note: Part of the international Hour-1 Bundle standard

points.label: Drowsiness + fever = danger
points.note: Altered consciousness is a sepsis marker — not just "high fever"

rf_groups_tr.note: Septic shock is life-threatening and progresses rapidly. Early antibiotic therapy and IV fluids are critical — every hour without treatment worsens outcomes.

rf_groups_tr.title: Acute Shortness of Breath
rf_groups_tr.action: Call 115 or go to ER immediately. Sit patient upright to ease breathing.
rf_groups_tr.keyFact: 💙 SpO2 < 90% = respiratory failure requiring immediate intervention. Blue lips and fingertips appear when SpO2 ≈ 85% — the body is severely oxygen-deprived. Sitting the patient upright (orthopnea position) allows better lung expansion than lying flat.
details: Common causes: (1) Acute pulmonary edema (heart attack, decompensated heart failure); (2) Pulmonary embolism (PE); (3) Severe asthma attack; (4) Pneumothorax; (5) Severe pneumonia; (6) Anaphylaxis.

Pulmonary embolism (PE): blood clot from deep leg veins travels to the lungs. Risk factors: prolonged immobility, post-surgery, cancer, pregnancy, long-haul flights. Symptoms: pleuritic chest pain + sudden shortness of breath + rapid heart rate.
Cyanosis (blue lips/fingernails) → SpO2 < 85% → immediate oxygen support needed. A finger pulse oximeter should be kept at home if any household member has asthma, COPD, or heart disease.

Severe asthma attack: unable to complete a sentence, SpO2 < 92%, respiratory rate > 30/min, accessory muscles in use. Administer salbutamol 2–4 puffs; if no response → call emergency services immediately.
Spontaneous pneumothorax: young, tall, thin person with sudden one-sided chest pain + shortness of breath. Tension pneumothorax must be treated within minutes — will not resolve on its own.

Anaphylaxis: breathing difficulty + hives/facial swelling after allergen exposure. Treatment: epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg intramuscular injection in the thigh immediately — the only life-saving intervention; antihistamines do not substitute.

points.label: SpO2 < 90% = respiratory failure
points.note: A finger pulse oximeter enables early home detection

points.label: Sitting upright helps lungs expand
points.note: Orthopnea position — do not force the patient to lie flat

points.label: Anaphylaxis: epinephrine IM immediately
points.note: Antihistamines cannot substitute epinephrine

points.label: Breathlessness after prolonged sitting = suspect PE
points.note: Pulmonary embolism may give no prior warning

rf_groups_tr.note: Pulmonary embolism can cause sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, and low oxygen saturation. Risk increases after prolonged immobility or surgery.

rf_soon_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Unintentional weight loss > 5% of body weight in 1 month (or > 10% in 6 months) is one of the most important "red flags" in medicine — it may be the first sign of cancer, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, or serious gastrointestinal disease.
details: Malignant causes to rule out: stomach cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, lymphoma, pancreatic cancer. These cancers often manifest with weight loss before other specific symptoms appear.

Endocrine causes: type 1 diabetes (rapid weight loss with excessive thirst and urination), hyperthyroidism (weight loss with palpitations, sweating, diarrhea), adrenal insufficiency (weight loss with fatigue, nausea, low blood pressure).
Gastrointestinal causes: Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, celiac disease (gluten intolerance), malabsorption syndrome. Often accompanied by chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, or abnormal stools.
Chronic infections: pulmonary tuberculosis (weight loss + cough + afternoon low-grade fever), HIV/AIDS, chronic parasitic infections. Ask about exposure history and travel.

What to bring to your doctor: weight measurements at multiple time points (self-monitored), food diary, accompanying symptoms. Your doctor will order: CBC, liver/kidney/thyroid function, glucose, and if needed — endoscopy or CT scan.

Intentional weight loss (dieting, exercise) is not a danger sign. Only be concerned when weight loss occurs WITHOUT changes in diet or activity — meaning the body is "consuming itself" due to an internal cause.

points.label: Warning threshold: > 5% in 1 month
points.note: Example: a 60 kg person losing > 3 kg for no clear reason

points.label: Rule out cancer first
points.note: Especially if > 45 years old or family history

points.label: Record weight and accompanying symptoms
points.note: Helps the doctor track trends and guide investigations

points.label: CBC + TSH + glucose as first step
points.note: Basic blood tests + endoscopy if indicated

rf_soon_tr.sign: Persistent fatigue > 2 weeks despite adequate sleep
rf_soon_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Persistent fatigue lasting > 6 weeks that does not improve despite adequate sleep and has no clear cause requires medical evaluation. Distinguish from ordinary tiredness: pathological fatigue does not recover with rest.
details: Anemia: the most common cause. Iron deficiency anemia (common in women with heavy periods, vegetarians), B12/folate deficiency (elderly, strict vegans). Symptoms: fatigue + pale skin + dizziness + rapid heartbeat.
Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH, low FT4. More common in women (5:1 ratio). Symptoms: fatigue + weight gain + cold intolerance + constipation + hair loss + dry skin. Diagnosed by TSH blood test.

Type 2 diabetes: high glucose → cells cannot use glucose → energy deficit. Also: excessive thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, slow wound healing. Many people first discover the disease through fatigue.

Depression and anxiety disorders: fatigue is a core symptom of depression. Often accompanied by insomnia/hypersomnia, loss of interest, sadness, difficulty concentrating. Mental health evaluation should run parallel to physical workup.

Myalgic encephalomyelitis/Chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS): severe fatigue > 6 months that worsens after exertion (post-exertional malaise), with brain fog and muscle/joint pain. A diagnosis of exclusion — after ruling out other causes.
Cancer: unexplained fatigue is a symptom of most cancers, especially lymphoma and leukemia. Particularly suspect if accompanied by weight loss, fever, and night sweats (B symptoms).

points.label: CBC + iron + TSH first
points.note: Anemia and hypothyroidism — common, treatable causes

points.label: Fasting blood glucose test
points.note: Type 2 diabetes is often discovered late through fatigue

points.label: Assess mental health
points.note: Depression and anxiety are very common causes of fatigue

points.label: Fatigue > 6 weeks without cause = see a doctor
points.note: Do not attribute it to "working too hard" and dismiss it

rf_soon_tr.sign: Frequent urination, excessive thirst, blurred vision
rf_soon_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Any new lump on the body or painless enlarged lymph node of unknown cause requires evaluation. Especially concerning: hard, immobile, irregularly bordered lumps, or lymph nodes > 2 cm persisting > 4 weeks.
details: Normal vs. abnormal lymph nodes: reactive nodes from infection are typically soft, tender, mobile, and shrink within 2–4 weeks. Concerning nodes: hard, painless, immobile, > 2 cm, persisting > 4 weeks, accompanied by weight loss/fever/night sweats.

Node location and significance: neck (throat infection, head and neck cancer, lymphoma); armpit (hand infection, breast cancer); groin (genital infection, lower limb melanoma); left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node — warning sign for abdominal cancer).

Lymphoma: Hodgkin's lymphoma is common in young adults 15–35, typically starting as painless neck nodes. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is more diverse, can occur at any age. B symptoms: fever, night sweats, weight loss.
Breast lump: any new lump in the breast requires evaluation — painful or not. Breast cancer is typically painless. Requires ultrasound (< 40 years) or mammography (> 40 years) and possibly biopsy.
Skin lesion — ABCDE signs: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter > 6mm, Evolution (change over time). Any changing mole needs examination.
Next steps: ultrasound or CT to assess size; FNA (fine needle aspiration) or excisional biopsy for histological diagnosis — this is the gold standard for determining malignant vs. benign.

points.label: Hard, painless, immobile node = concerning
points.note: Unlike reactive nodes: soft, tender, shrinking within 2–4 weeks

points.label: Left supraclavicular node = high alert
points.note: Virchow's node — often linked to abdominal cancer

points.label: Ultrasound is the first step
points.note: Fast, affordable, no radiation — assesses structure and size

points.label: Biopsy = definitive diagnosis
points.note: Only biopsy can distinguish benign from malignant

rf_soon_tr.sign: Persistent cough > 3 weeks or bloody phlegm
rf_soon_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Blood in the urine (hematuria) — even once, painless, with no other symptoms — requires medical evaluation. Painless hematuria in a person > 45 years old should be considered bladder or kidney cancer until ruled out.
details: Gross hematuria (visible to the naked eye): urine is red or brown. Microscopic hematuria (laboratory finding): > 3 red blood cells per high-power field. Both require evaluation — microscopic hematuria can also indicate serious disease.

Causes by age: young (< 40): glomerulonephritis (IgA nephropathy), kidney stones, urinary tract infection. Middle-aged and older (> 45): bladder cancer and kidney cancer are the top priorities to rule out.

Bladder cancer: common in men > 50 years, smokers, those exposed to industrial chemicals. Painless hematuria is the first symptom in 80% of cases. Best outcomes when detected at an early stage (confined to the mucosa).
Kidney stones: hematuria accompanied by severe colicky pain (renal colic) radiating from flank to groin. Non-contrast CT scan is the diagnostic standard (95% sensitivity).
Glomerulonephritis: microscopic hematuria + proteinuria + edema. IgA nephropathy is common in young adults after respiratory infections. Kidney biopsy is needed for diagnosis and damage assessment.
What to do: urinalysis (UA) is the first step; if hematuria is confirmed → kidney and bladder ultrasound, urine cytology, and if > 45 years → cystoscopy.

points.label: Painless hematuria > 45 years = rule out cancer first
points.note: 80% of bladder cancers present with painless hematuria

points.label: Urinalysis is the first step
points.note: Confirms hematuria and looks for signs of infection/inflammation

points.label: Ultrasound + CT of urinary tract
points.note: Detects stones, kidney tumors, structural abnormalities

points.label: Cystoscopy if > 45 years
points.note: Gold standard for detecting early-stage bladder cancer

rf_soon_tr.sign: New painless lump anywhere on the body
rf_soon_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ A cough lasting > 3 weeks not caused by a cold or not improving with standard treatment requires ruling out pulmonary tuberculosis, lung cancer, and chronic lung disease. Especially concerning if accompanied by coughing up blood, weight loss, or prolonged fever.
details: Pulmonary tuberculosis: chronic cough + afternoon low-grade fever + night sweats + weight loss is the classic tetrad. Vietnam is among the 30 countries with the highest TB burden globally. Diagnosis: chest X-ray + sputum AFB (3 samples) + GeneXpert MTB/RIF.

Lung cancer: usually asymptomatic in early stages. Warning signs: new-onset cough or change in cough character in smokers, coughing up blood, hoarseness, chest pain. 5-year survival: stage I > 90%, stage IV only 10%.

ACE inhibitor-induced cough: dry, irritating cough occurring in 5–20% of people on antihypertensive ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril, lisinopril). Cough usually resolves 1–4 weeks after stopping the medication.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD): chronic cough at night or after meals, with acid reflux and heartburn. Mechanism: acid irritates the larynx/bronchi. A 4–8-week trial of PPI therapy with improvement is diagnostically valuable.

Cough-variant asthma: persistent dry cough, worse at night and early morning, triggered by cold/exertion/chemical odors. No obvious wheeze. Diagnosed by spirometry and bronchodilator reversibility test.

Post-nasal drip: nasal secretions drip down the throat → irritating cough, common in chronic sinusitis. More cough in the morning, sensation of fluid running down the back of the throat. Treatment: nasal corticosteroid spray, antihistamines.

points.label: Rule out pulmonary TB first in Vietnam
points.note: Chest X-ray + sputum AFB + GeneXpert — if cough > 3 weeks

points.label: Smoker + new cough = suspect lung cancer
points.note: Low-dose CT screening for lung cancer for smokers > 50

points.label: Check current medications
points.note: ACE inhibitors cause dry cough — stopping the drug is the treatment

points.label: Chest X-ray is the first step
points.note: Fast, affordable, rules out TB and major lung abnormalities

rf_soon_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Persistent black stools or ongoing bright red blood in stool — not attributable to known constipation or hemorrhoids — requires ruling out colorectal cancer and gastrointestinal bleeding. Pencil-thin stools persisting over time are a warning sign of rectal cancer.
details: Black stools (melena): tar-like black, distinctive odor — upper gastrointestinal bleeding (stomach, duodenum). Causes: peptic ulcer, esophageal varices (liver cirrhosis). Urgent gastroscopy needed if black stools accompany dizziness or fainting.

Bright red blood in stool (hematochezia): usually lower GI bleeding. Benign causes: hemorrhoids, anal fissure. Serious causes: colon polyps, colorectal cancer, colitis. Do not assume hemorrhoids without endoscopic confirmation.

Colorectal cancer: alternating constipation and diarrhea, narrower stools, blood in stool, abdominal pain, weight loss are the classic tetrad. The world's 3rd most common cancer; > 90% survival if detected at stage I.
Colorectal cancer screening: ACS recommends starting at age 45 with: colonoscopy every 10 years, or fecal immunochemical test (FIT) annually, or stool DNA testing every 3 years.
Pencil-thin stools persisting over time: a tumor in the rectum narrows the bowel lumen — stool is compressed into a pencil shape. This is a high-alert warning sign requiring immediate colonoscopy.

Medications causing stool color changes: iron and bismuth cause black stools (without the distinctive melena odor); beets and red foods can cause red stools. Ask about medications and foods first — but it is still best to get checked.

points.label: Black stool + dizziness = emergency
points.note: Upper GI bleeding can cause rapid blood loss

points.label: Pencil-thin stools = suspect rectal cancer
points.note: Tumor narrows the bowel — colonoscopy immediately

points.label: Do not assume it is hemorrhoids
points.note: Hemorrhoids cause bright red blood — but so does cancer. Endoscopy confirms.

points.label: Screening from age 45
points.note: Colonoscopy every 10 years or FIT test annually

rf_soon_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Severe headache upon waking in the early morning (often relieved by vomiting), with projectile vomiting and visual changes — is the classic sign of raised intracranial pressure. May indicate a brain tumor, intracranial hematoma, or hydrocephalus requiring urgent diagnosis.
details: Raised intracranial pressure (RICP): the Cushing triad — early morning headache (worst upon waking, improves after standing/vomiting), projectile vomiting (without preceding nausea), papilledema (blurred vision, double vision). Normal pressure: 5–15 mmHg; RICP when > 20 mmHg.

Primary brain tumors: glioblastoma (grade IV, rapidly progressive, median survival 15 months), meningioma (usually benign, slow-growing). Not all brain tumors cause headaches — only 50% have headache as a symptom.

Brain metastases: most commonly from lung cancer (50%), breast cancer (15%), colorectal cancer, kidney cancer. Progressive headache with focal neurological deficits (one-sided limb weakness, visual disturbance, personality changes).

Hydrocephalus: accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid → raised pressure. Acquired forms (after meningitis, after subarachnoid hemorrhage). Symptoms: progressively worsening headache, drowsiness, unsteady gait.

Differentiating from benign migraine: migraine can also be severe in the morning and accompanied by vomiting — but has an aura, known triggers, and a long history. A "worst headache of my life" (thunderclap headache) is an emergency — think of ruptured aneurysm.

What to do: MRI brain with/without contrast is the gold standard. CT brain is more appropriate in emergencies (fast, detects bleeding well). Do not delay if accompanied by new limb weakness, seizures, or altered consciousness.

points.label: Early morning headache + projectile vomiting = RICP
points.note: Raised intracranial pressure — do not self-treat

points.label: "Worst headache of my life" = emergency
points.note: Thunderclap headache — suspect ruptured cerebral aneurysm

points.label: Brain MRI is the gold standard
points.note: Better than CT for small tumors — CT used in emergencies

points.label: Progressive headache ≠ migraine
points.note: Gets worse every day, does not respond to standard medication

rf_soon_tr.sign: Mole changing colour, size, or shape (ABCDE rule)
rf_soon_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Sudden vision loss or persistent double vision is a serious neurological or eye emergency. Sudden loss of vision in one eye (amaurosis fugax) may represent a TIA and predicts stroke within the following 48 hours.
details: Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss): complete loss of vision in one eye lasting seconds to minutes, then self-resolving — like "a curtain coming down." Cause: temporary blockage of retinal blood supply by an embolus from carotid artery atherosclerosis. This is an ocular TIA — neurovascular emergency.

Retinal detachment: partial vision loss (as if a curtain covers one corner of the visual field), with flashing lights and more floaters than usual. Painless. Requires urgent surgery within 24 hours if the macula is unaffected — delay causes permanent blindness.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma: sudden spike in intraocular pressure → severe eye pain + blurred vision + halos around lights + nausea. Ophthalmological emergency — high pressure causes irreversible damage to the optic nerve.

Double vision (diplopia) classification: monocular (covering the other eye still causes double vision) → eye problem. Binocular (covering one eye resolves the diplopia) → neurological cause. Cranial nerve III, IV, or VI palsy → suspect aneurysm, brain tumor, raised intracranial pressure.
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO): "eye stroke" — sudden, complete, painless loss of vision in one eye. Treatment window < 4–6 hours. Must go to emergency room immediately, like a brain stroke.

Distinguishing from benign causes: blurring due to refractive error (improves when squinting), blurring when looking at distance (simple myopia). Concerning when: one eye affected, sudden onset, accompanied by eye pain, or not improving with rest.

points.label: Transient monocular blindness = TIA = emergency
points.note: Risk of stroke in the next 48 hours — call emergency services

points.label: "Curtain" over vision = suspect retinal detachment
points.note: Surgery within 24h if macula unaffected — delay causes blindness

points.label: Binocular double vision = neurological cause
points.note: If covering one eye resolves it → brain/nerve problem

points.label: Eye pain + halos around lights = acute glaucoma
points.note: Ophthalmological emergency — optic nerve damage is irreversible

rf_prep_tr.title: Memorise 115 (Emergency)
rf_prep_tr.desc: Programme it into your phone for quick access
rf_prep_tr.keyFact: ✅ In an emergency, the panicking brain cannot recall phone numbers — even ones memorised long ago. Saving "115 Emergency" with a clear display name means anyone holding the phone can call immediately.
details: Why save rather than memorise: research on acute stress shows the prefrontal cortex — the region handling memory and decision-making — is strongly suppressed during "fight or flight". Even the simplest action (calling a saved number) remains possible even while panicking.
Save with a clear name: "115 Emergency" or "SOS – Emergency 115". If your phone has an ICE (In Case of Emergency) feature, add the contact information of a close family member.

Enable SOS emergency feature: iOS — press the power button 5 times or hold power + volume button for automatic SOS call. Android — varies by manufacturer, usually in Settings → Safety and emergency → Emergency SOS.

Medical ID (iOS) / Emergency information (Android): enter blood type, drug allergies, chronic conditions, emergency contact. This information appears on the lock screen — emergency responders can read it without unlocking the phone.
Teach the whole family: children as young as 5–6 can learn to call emergency services with guidance. Practice with role-play scenarios: "If mum/dad falls and cannot get up, what would you do?"

Beyond 115: also save the number of the nearest hospital emergency department, a reliable local taxi service (if needed to transport quickly when 115 is busy), and the numbers of at least 2 family members who can arrive within 15 minutes.

points.label: Panicking brain cannot recall numbers
points.note: Save in advance — the simplest life-saving action

points.label: Medical ID shows on lock screen
points.note: Emergency responders can read it without unlocking the phone

points.label: Teach children from age 5–6
points.note: Practise emergency role-play scenarios with children

points.label: Also save hospital + family members
points.note: At least 2 people who can arrive within 15 minutes

rf_prep_tr.title: First Aid Kit
rf_prep_tr.desc: Antiseptic, bandages, thermometer, blood pressure cuff
rf_prep_tr.keyFact: 🏥 "Door-to-needle time" for stroke and "door-to-balloon time" for heart attack are medical quality standards — every minute from hospital arrival counts. Knowing in advance which facility is nearby and capable of handling emergencies shortens decision time when you are panicking.
details: Types of medical facilities: local health station — basic first aid, no surgery. District hospital — basic emergency care, some surgeries. Provincial hospital — ICU, complex surgeries, stroke unit. Specialty hospitals (major centres) — most critical cases.

Capabilities to know in advance: (1) Does it have a 24/7 emergency department? (2) Does it have a stroke unit? (3) Does it have coronary intervention (PCI)? — critical for heart attack. (4) Does it have an operating room active 24/7?

List 2–3 hospitals by distance: (1) Nearest (< 10 min) — for any emergency; (2) Nearest hospital with a stroke unit / PCI; (3) Specialist hospital if transfer is needed. Save addresses in Google Maps for immediate navigation.

Traffic and alternate routes: know the route during rush hour. Some hospitals have a separate emergency entrance — not the main gate. Find out in advance and save the GPS coordinates of the emergency entrance.

Health insurance and coverage: the national health insurance pays at the correct referral tier. True emergencies (life-threatening) are covered at any tier including out-of-network — but valid documentation is required.

Create a family emergency plan: post on the refrigerator or front door — list of hospitals, phone numbers, addresses, emergency contacts. Especially important if elderly, young children, or chronically ill persons are in the household.

points.label: Every minute from hospital arrival counts
points.note: Door-to-needle (stroke) and door-to-balloon (cardiac) are gold standards

points.label: Save GPS coordinates of the emergency entrance
points.note: Emergency entrance is often different from the main gate — find out in advance

points.label: True emergencies are covered out-of-network
points.note: But documentation and emergency confirmation from the hospital are required

points.label: Post an emergency plan at home
points.note: On the fridge or front door — visible to everyone immediately

rf_prep_tr.title: FAST Rule for Stroke
rf_prep_tr.desc: Face drooping · Arm weakness · Speech difficulty · Time to call 115
rf_prep_tr.keyFact: 🎒 An emergency kit is not a complex survival kit — just 5 essentials in one small bag in a fixed location: (1) Aspirin 300mg, (2) List of current medications + allergies, (3) ID card, (4) Health insurance card, (5) Emergency contact numbers. Prepared = saves 5–10 minutes in a situation where every minute has value.
details: Aspirin 300mg: chew immediately when a heart attack is suspected (if not allergic). Standard dose: 300mg chewed (not swallowed whole) → absorbed 50% faster. Do not use if allergic to aspirin, actively bleeding from the GI tract, or uncertain about stroke type. Check expiry date every 6 months.

Medication list: write drug name, dose, frequency, prescribing doctor. Especially important: anticoagulants (warfarin, rivaroxaban, dabigatran), insulin, cardiac medications, anticonvulsants. Emergency responders need this to avoid dangerous drug interactions.

Allergy list: clearly note drug allergies (penicillin, aspirin, NSAIDs), severe food allergies (peanuts, seafood), iodine contrast dye allergy (important if CT/MRI with contrast is needed). Include the specific reaction (hives vs. anaphylaxis).

Personal documents: national ID card (needed for hospital admission and identity verification), health insurance card (or VssID/VNeID app as a digital alternative), credit card / small amount of cash (hospital deposit). Photograph everything and save on your phone as a backup.

Personal emergency medications: asthma — salbutamol inhaler (Ventolin); diabetes — glucose tablets (dextrose) for hypoglycaemia; severe allergy — epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) if prescribed; cardiac — nitroglycerin spray/sublingual if prescribed.

Location and storage: keep the emergency bag in a FIXED location that everyone in the household knows. Check every 6 months: drug expiry dates, document validity, update medication list. Do not keep in the car — high temperatures damage medications.

points.label: Aspirin 300mg — chew when heart attack suspected
points.note: Check expiry date every 6 months

points.label: Medication list + allergies = most important
points.note: Helps emergency responders avoid dangerous drug interactions

points.label: ID + insurance card + small cash
points.note: Photograph everything and save on your phone as a backup

points.label: Fixed location — everyone in the household knows
points.note: Check and update every 6 months

rf_prep_tr.title: Emergency Contacts List
rf_prep_tr.desc: Keep visible at home — especially for elderly or solo residents
rf_prep_tr.keyFact: 💪 CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) increases survival after sudden cardiac arrest from 5% to 40–50% when performed correctly within the first 4 minutes. Every minute without CPR = 10% less chance of survival. You do not need to be a doctor — basic CPR can be learned in 30 minutes.
details: Recognising cardiac arrest: unresponsive person (does not react to voice or touch), not breathing normally (no breath or gasping — agonal breathing). Do not check for pulse — untrained people checking a pulse take 5–10 seconds and are usually wrong. If unsure whether the person is breathing normally → start CPR.

Chain of Survival: (1) Recognition and calling emergency services; (2) Early high-quality CPR; (3) Early AED (automated external defibrillator); (4) Advanced emergency care; (5) Post-cardiac arrest care. CPR and AED are the two links you can action before emergency services arrive.

CPR technique: (1) Place victim on their back on a hard, flat surface; (2) Kneel beside them at chest level; (3) Place two hands overlapping in the centre of the lower chest (sternum); (4) Compress 5–6 cm deep at 100–120 per minute (at the beat of "Stayin' Alive" by the Bee Gees); (5) Allow full chest recoil between compressions; (6) Do not stop unless relieved or AED arrives.

Rescue breathing: according to AHA 2020, compression-only CPR (Hands-Only CPR) is sufficient for adults with sudden cardiac arrest from a cardiac cause in the first 5–10 minutes. Rescue breathing is more important for: children, drowning, poisoning, respiratory-cause arrest.

AED (Automated External Defibrillator): device that automatically analyses heart rhythm and provides voice guidance. Only shocks if it detects ventricular fibrillation (VF/VT) — will not shock normal rhythm or asystole. Find AEDs: airports, shopping centres, gyms, some office buildings. Learn to use one before you need it.

Where to learn CPR: the AHA / Vietnamese Heart Association runs BLS (Basic Life Support) courses — 4 hours, certificate valid 2 years. Many hospitals run free community classes. Watching AHA tutorial videos on YouTube is a temporary measure — but does not replace hands-on practice on a manikin.

points.label: Every minute without CPR = −10% survival
points.note: Start immediately — imperfect CPR is better than none

points.label: 100–120 per minute = beat of "Stayin' Alive"
points.note: The Bee Gees' song has exactly the right CPR rhythm

points.label: Find AEDs in public places
points.note: Airports, shopping centres, gyms — learn to use one in advance

points.label: BLS course 4 hours = 2-year certificate
points.note: AHA / Vietnamese Heart Association — many free classes available

rf_prep_tr.title: Basic First Aid Skills
rf_prep_tr.desc: CPR, wound care, recovery position — learn at community level

med_rules_tr.title: Never change medication or dose on your own
med_rules_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Every prescription is chosen based on a specific patient profile — diagnosis, underlying conditions, current medications, liver/kidney function, and allergies. "Looks the same" does not mean the same active ingredient or equivalent dose. Changing medication on your own is gambling with your health.
details: Generic vs. brand: generic and brand-name drugs contain the same active ingredient and dose but may differ in excipients, coating, and release mechanism — affecting absorption and efficacy. Sensitive drugs (levothyroxine, warfarin, anticonvulsants) should not be switched between generic and brand without consulting a doctor.

Reducing dose when "feeling better": especially dangerous with antibiotics (creates resistance), corticosteroids (acute adrenal insufficiency if stopped abruptly), antidepressants (discontinuation syndrome), and cardiac medications (rebound tachycardia).

Drug-drug interactions (P450 enzyme effects): warfarin + many antibiotics → increased bleeding risk; statins + clarithromycin → increased rhabdomyolysis risk; ACE inhibitor + NSAIDs → acute kidney injury.

Look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) medications: drug errors due to similar names or appearance are among the leading causes of medication errors in hospitals and at home. ISMP maintains a list of dangerous LASA drug pairs.

If you want to switch or reduce dose: always discuss with the prescribing doctor. Many doctors are willing to adjust if you explain your reason (cost, side effects, inconvenience). Do not self-decide because "I read online that someone else does it this way".

Antibiotics and completing the full course: symptoms improve before bacteria are fully eliminated. Stopping antibiotics early → surviving bacteria develop resistance → next relapse is harder to treat. This is the main mechanism creating antibiotic-resistant superbugs.

points.label: Generic ≠ automatic substitution
points.note: Sensitive drugs (warfarin, levothyroxine) — ask doctor before switching

points.label: Stopping corticosteroids abruptly is dangerous
points.note: Acute adrenal insufficiency — taper dose gradually as directed

points.label: P450 interactions — read the package insert
points.note: Warfarin, statins, ACE inhibitors are most prone to interactions

points.label: Ask your doctor instead of self-adjusting
points.note: Doctors will adjust if you explain your reason

med_rules_tr.desc: Do not substitute prescription medications with supplements, herbs, or over-the-counter alternatives without consulting your doctor. Active ingredients differ significantly.

med_rules_tr.title: Take at the correct time and in the correct way
med_rules_tr.keyFact: ⏱️ Medication timing is not arbitrary — it is determined by pharmacokinetics: absorption rate, the effect of food on gastric pH, and the need to maintain therapeutic blood levels. Taking medication at the wrong time can reduce efficacy by up to 50% or increase side effects.
details: Take on an empty stomach: levothyroxine (40% better absorption when fasting); omeprazole/PPIs (need to be activated 30 minutes before a meal); bisphosphonates (alendronate — take fasting with a full glass of water, stay upright for 30 minutes after).

Take with food: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin — reduces gastric mucosal irritation); metformin (reduces nausea and diarrhea when taken with meals); iron — better absorbed fasting but can be taken with a light meal if intolerance occurs.

Antibiotics and consistent dosing: time-dependent antibiotics (penicillin, amoxicillin, cephalosporins) need blood levels maintained above the MIC throughout the dosing interval. Taking 2–3 hours late → levels drop below MIC → bacteria regrow.

Evening medications: statins (atorvastatin can be taken anytime; simvastatin/pravastatin best at night because the liver synthesises most cholesterol between 2–4 AM); antihypertensives (MAPEC/TIME studies suggest evening dosing reduces cardiovascular events).

Extended-release formulations (XR/SR/XL): do NOT crush or split — this destroys the release mechanism → entire dose released at once → possible overdose toxicity. Examples: metoprolol XL, metformin XR, nifedipine SR, lithium SR.

Taking with water: most medications should be taken with at least 200 ml of water (one full glass) to ensure the tablet reaches the stomach and dissolves properly. Bisphosphonates require 250 ml. Do not take with orange juice, coffee, or milk — these affect absorption.

points.label: Levothyroxine: take fasting — important
points.note: Food and calcium reduce absorption by 40% — take 30–60 min before eating

points.label: Do not crush/split XR/SR/XL tablets
points.note: Destroys the release mechanism → risk of acute overdose

points.label: Antibiotics: same time every day
points.note: Late dose → levels drop → bacteria regrow

points.label: Take with at least 200 ml of water
points.note: Not with milk, orange juice, or coffee — affects absorption

med_rules_tr.desc: Some medications must be taken before meals (on an empty stomach) to be absorbed properly; others must be taken after meals to avoid stomach irritation. Always follow the label.

med_rules_tr.title: Be aware of food-drug interactions
med_rules_tr.keyFact: 🍊 Grapefruit (and some other foods) does more than "slightly affect" medications — it can raise drug blood levels 2–10 fold, equivalent to taking an overdose. Food-drug interactions are often overlooked but can be far more dangerous than most people realise.
details: Grapefruit and CYP3A4: grapefruit contains furanocoumarins that inhibit the intestinal CYP3A4 enzyme — the enzyme that metabolises 50% of common medications. The effect lasts 24–72 hours after a single glass of grapefruit juice. Most dangerous combinations: statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin → rhabdomyolysis risk), calcium channel blockers (felodipine, nifedipine → excessive blood pressure drop), immunosuppressants (cyclosporine → nephrotoxicity), sildenafil (Viagra → dangerous hypotension).

Alcohol + paracetamol: regular drinkers have increased CYP2E1 activity → more paracetamol converted to NAPQI (hepatotoxic metabolite); glutathione (the detoxifier) is also depleted by alcohol. The safe limit drops to 2g/day (instead of 4g). Paracetamol is still a better pain choice than NSAIDs in drinkers if used at the correct dose.

Vitamin K and warfarin: green leafy vegetables rich in vitamin K (kale, broccoli, spinach) affect warfarin efficacy. No need to eliminate them — but keep intake consistent (do not suddenly increase or decrease). Inform your doctor if you change your diet so the warfarin dose can be adjusted.

Milk and antibiotics: calcium in dairy forms chelate complexes with tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) → reduces absorption by 40–90%. Take these antibiotics at least 2 hours apart from dairy products and antacids containing calcium, magnesium, or aluminium.

Tyramine and MAOIs: monoamine oxidase inhibitors (some antidepressants) + tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, red wine, cured meats, soy sauce, miso) → hypertensive crisis, life-threatening. Ask your pharmacist if you are on an MAOI.

Caffeine and medications: caffeine + fluoroquinolone antibiotics (ciprofloxacin) → elevated caffeine levels → anxiety, palpitations. Caffeine + ephedrine (some cold medicines) → elevated heart rate and blood pressure. Taking medications with coffee is generally not recommended.

points.label: Grapefruit effect lasts 24–72 hours
points.note: Not just "taken at the same time" — still active the next day

points.label: Alcohol + paracetamol = dangerous
points.note: Safe limit drops to 2g/day in regular drinkers

points.label: Milk + tetracycline/ciprofloxacin: 2-hour gap
points.note: Calcium chelates with antibiotics → reduces absorption 40–90%

points.label: Vitamin K + warfarin: stay consistent
points.note: No need to avoid green vegetables — just eat them consistently

med_rules_tr.desc: Grapefruit inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme responsible for metabolising many drugs (statins, blood pressure meds, some antibiotics), causing dangerously high blood concentrations.

med_rules_tr.title: Never share prescription medications
med_rules_tr.keyFact: 🚫 Even when symptoms look identical, the underlying cause may be completely different — and the same drug can cause serious harm due to underlying conditions, drug interactions, or allergies that the prescribing doctor did not know about in your case.
details: Same symptoms ≠ same disease: a headache may be migraine, high blood pressure, a brain tumour, or stress — treatments differ. Abdominal pain may be a peptic ulcer, kidney stone, or appendicitis. The drug that works for someone else may not work for you without knowing the cause.

Cross-reactivity (allergic): patients with penicillin allergy have a 1–10% chance of cross-reacting with cephalosporins. Aspirin-allergic patients may be allergic to all NSAIDs. Sulfonamide-allergic patients may react to furosemide and thiazide diuretics. Not knowing someone else's allergy profile means not knowing if their medication is safe for you.

Weight- and age-based dosing: paracetamol, ibuprofen, many antibiotics are dosed by body weight in kg — especially important in children and the elderly. A dose for a 70 kg adult is not suitable for a 45 kg person or a child.

Interactions with your current medications: the person giving you their medication does not know what you are already taking. Example: they give you clarithromycin (antibiotic) but you are on simvastatin → dangerous interaction increasing rhabdomyolysis risk.

Underlying conditions affect drug choice: NSAIDs (ibuprofen) are contraindicated in kidney failure, active peptic ulcer, and heart failure. Metformin is contraindicated when GFR < 30. Quinolones affect cartilage in children. The person sharing the drug does not know your contraindications.

Antibiotics and resistance: using antibiotics without the right indication (viruses do not need antibiotics), without completing the course, or using the wrong type for the bacteria → selective pressure creates resistant strains. Vietnam has one of the world's highest antibiotic resistance rates due to over-the-counter antibiotic overuse.

points.label: Same symptoms ≠ same disease
points.note: Headaches and abdominal pain have dozens of different causes

points.label: Cross-reactivity — hidden danger
points.note: Penicillin allergy → possible cephalosporin cross-reaction

points.label: Weight-based dosing — especially children
points.note: Adult 70 kg dose is unsuitable for children or smaller individuals

points.label: Vietnam: top antibiotic resistance globally
points.note: Consequence of widespread over-the-counter antibiotic use

med_rules_tr.desc: Medication prescribed for another person — even if symptoms seem similar — may be inappropriate for your condition, weight, or other medications you take. Never share prescriptions.

med_rules_tr.title: Store medications correctly
med_rules_tr.keyFact: 🌡️ Temperature and humidity can break down the chemical structure of medications — not only reducing efficacy but creating harmful degradation products. Bathrooms (humid, warm) and cars (up to 70°C in summer) are the two most common places that damage medications.
details: Standard storage conditions: "room temperature" per pharmacopoeia = 15–25°C, humidity < 60%. "Cool" = 8–15°C. "Refrigerated" = 2–8°C (refrigerator shelf, NOT frozen). "Frozen" = below −10°C. Read the drug label for specific requirements.

Insulin: unopened vials/pens → refrigerator 2–8°C. In-use vials/pens → room temperature below 25°C, maximum 28–30 days (depending on type). Do not freeze (frozen insulin loses potency). Do not place near the refrigerator exhaust (temperature too low). Always read the package insert for each insulin type.

Tablet medications and high temperature: gelatin capsules, suppositories, and some creams are heat-sensitive. A car parked outdoors in summer can reach 60–80°C inside — enough to degrade many medications within hours. Do not leave medications in the glove compartment or boot.

Bathroom — the worst environment: high humidity (steam from shower/bath) + temperature fluctuations → moisture absorption breaks tablet coatings, hydrolyses active ingredients, promotes mould growth. A medicine cabinet in the bathroom is a common habit but inappropriate.

Light and oxidation: UV and visible light oxidise many active ingredients (especially vitamins A, C, E, some antibiotics like doxycycline, tetracycline). This is why many drugs come in dark-coloured containers. Do not remove medications from original packaging unless necessary.

Expired medications: most are still safe after the expiry date but have reduced potency. Dangerous exceptions: expired tetracycline → kidney toxicity (Fanconi syndrome); expired nitroglycerin → loses potency in a cardiac emergency; expired insulin → reduced blood glucose control. Dispose of expired drugs correctly: do not flush — return to a pharmacy or medical facility.

points.label: Cars can reach 60–80°C in summer
points.note: Degrades many medications in hours — do not leave in the car

points.label: Bathroom = worst environment for medications
points.note: Humidity + heat → hydrolysis, mould, reduced potency

points.label: Insulin in use: room temperature ≤ 30 days
points.note: Do not freeze — frozen insulin loses potency completely

points.label: Do not flush expired medications
points.note: Return to a pharmacy or medical facility for proper disposal

med_rules_tr.desc: Most medications should be stored in a cool, dry place away from sunlight. Humidity and heat (e.g. bathroom cabinets) accelerate degradation and reduce effectiveness.

med_danger_tr.risk: Overdose, organ toxicity depending on drug type
med_danger_tr.keyFact: 🚨 Drug doses are calculated based on pharmacokinetics — the gap between the therapeutic dose and the toxic dose (therapeutic index) is often very narrow. Increasing the dose does not mean "recovering faster" — it means approaching the threshold for organ damage.
details: Narrow therapeutic index: drugs such as digoxin, warfarin, lithium, phenytoin, and theophylline have a very small margin between therapeutic and toxic dose — doubling the dose can cause serious toxicity from even a slight increase.

Paracetamol — the most common trap: at therapeutic doses, the liver safely metabolises paracetamol. With overdose, the main pathway becomes saturated → CYP2E1 generates NAPQI (a potent toxin). Glutathione used to neutralise NAPQI is depleted → irreversible liver cell damage develops after 3–5 days.

NSAID overdose (ibuprofen, naproxen): acute gastric ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, acute kidney injury (prostaglandin inhibition → renal vasoconstriction), and above 3,200 mg/day of ibuprofen, increased stroke and heart attack risk.

High-dose vitamin D over time: many people increase the dose because "I'm vitamin D deficient so more is better". Vitamin D > 10,000 IU/day long-term → hypercalcaemia (high blood calcium) → nausea, kidney stones, soft tissue calcification, cardiac arrhythmia. Measure 25(OH)D blood levels before adjusting doses.

Antibiotics at higher dose do not cure faster: antibiotic efficacy (except concentration-dependent groups like aminoglycosides) depends on the time blood levels remain above MIC, not the peak level. Increasing amoxicillin dose does not kill bacteria faster — only increases diarrhoea and disrupts beneficial gut bacteria.

Overdose symptoms requiring emergency care: severe nausea/vomiting after taking medication, severe abdominal pain, jaundice (liver damage), little or no urine output (kidney failure), altered consciousness, seizures. If drug poisoning is suspected: call emergency services or go to A&E immediately — do not wait for symptoms to worsen.

points.label: Narrow therapeutic index — very dangerous
points.note: Digoxin, warfarin, lithium, phenytoin — small dose increase = toxicity

points.label: Paracetamol: NAPQI damages liver after 3–5 days
points.note: Overdose is painless at first — silent damage until too late

points.label: Vitamin D > 10,000 IU/day → kidney stones
points.note: Measure 25(OH)D blood level before self-increasing to high doses

points.label: Suspected drug poisoning → call emergency now
points.note: Do not wait for symptoms to worsen — treatment window is very narrow

med_danger_tr.risk: Natural ≠ safe; toxicity, interactions, contamination possible
med_danger_tr.keyFact: 🌿 "Natural" does not mean "safe." Many herbs contain potent pharmacological compounds, interact with prescription drugs, and have not undergone rigorous clinical trials before going to market.
details: St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) — the most notorious disruptor: potent inducer of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein → reduces levels of dozens of important drugs: HIV medications (indinavir reduced by 57%), oral contraceptives (may lead to unintended pregnancy), warfarin (reduced anticoagulant effect), cyclosporine (increased transplant rejection risk), digoxin, many antidepressants.

Kava (Piper methysticum) and liver toxicity: kava is a popular herb for anxiety relief. However, over 100 cases of acute liver failure and deaths have been reported globally, leading to bans in Germany, Switzerland, and Canada. Combined with alcohol or sedatives → increased risk of respiratory depression.

Aristolochic acid (in some traditional Asian medicine herbs): a potent nephrotoxin and proven carcinogen (IARC Group 1). Has caused thousands of cases of chronic kidney failure (Belgian herbal nephropathy) and is associated with urothelial cancer. Banned in many countries but still circulates in some markets.
Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) in comfrey, coltsfoot, borage: hepatotoxic compounds causing hepatic veno-occlusive disease, especially dangerous in children and pregnant women.

Contamination and adulteration in herbal products: many analyses of herbal supplements have found heavy metals (lead, mercury, arsenic — especially in traditional Chinese medicine from China), undisclosed pharmaceutical ingredients (sildenafil in "male enhancement" products, sibutramine in weight-loss products, corticosteroids in "herbal joint" preparations), and unlisted active compounds.

Common herb-drug interactions: high-dose garlic + warfarin → increased bleeding; ginger + aspirin → increased bleeding; ginseng + warfarin → affects INR; fish oil > 3g/day + warfarin → increased bleeding risk. Always inform your doctor about all herbs you are taking.

points.label: St. John's Wort reduces HIV drug by 57%
points.note: Also inactivates oral contraceptives, warfarin, and cyclosporine

points.label: Kava → acute liver failure, banned in many countries
points.note: Combined with alcohol/sedatives → respiratory depression risk

points.label: Aristolochic acid → chronic kidney failure, cancer
points.note: IARC Group 1 — confirmed carcinogen

points.label: Herbal supplements: verify the source
points.note: Heavy metal contamination and hidden ingredients are more common than you think

med_danger_tr.phrase: 'Doctors don't want you to know this'
med_danger_tr.risk: Conspiracy framing to bypass critical thinking
med_danger_tr.keyFact: 🦠 Vietnam is among the countries with the highest antibiotic resistance rates in the world. Stopping antibiotics early when "feeling better" is one of the main drivers of drug-resistant superbugs.
details: Why symptoms resolve before bacteria are eliminated: the immune system and antibiotics work together — symptoms improve when bacteria drop below the disease-causing threshold, but resistant survivors remain. These bacteria thrive when antibiotics are stopped.

Mechanism of selective resistance pressure: bacterial populations always contain random variants. Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria, leaving those with resistance traits. If stopped too early, these resistant bacteria multiply and become a new strain that is harder to treat.

Resistance in Vietnam: studies record MRSA (methicillin-resistant S. aureus) at 30–40% of isolates; E. coli resistance to fluoroquinolones > 60%; carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is rising — the "last resort" antibiotics are gradually losing effectiveness.

Antibiotics do not kill viruses — a common cause of resistance: 70–80% of common colds, flu, and pharyngitis are viral. Antibiotics are completely ineffective against viruses but still kill beneficial gut bacteria, creating opportunities for resistant strains to colonise.

Time-dependent vs. concentration-dependent antibiotics: time-dependent (penicillin, amoxicillin, cephalosporins, metronidazole) work when levels are maintained above the MIC throughout the dosing interval. Taking a dose 2–4 hours late → levels drop below MIC → bacteria regrow during that window. This is why taking at the right time and completing the full course matters.

Superbugs and global consequences: the WHO lists antibiotic resistance as one of the 10 greatest global health threats. By 2050, antibiotic resistance could cause 10 million deaths per year — surpassing cancer. Every early antibiotic stop contributes to this global crisis.

points.label: Symptom-free ≠ bacteria-free
points.note: Resistant bacteria remain — stopping early lets them multiply

points.label: Vietnam: MRSA 30–40%, E. coli FQ resistance 60%+
points.note: Among the highest antibiotic resistance rates in the world

points.label: Viruses do not need antibiotics
points.note: 70–80% of colds/flu/pharyngitis are viral — antibiotics are useless

points.label: By 2050: 10 million deaths/year from superbugs
points.note: Every incorrect antibiotic use contributes to this global crisis

med_danger_tr.risk: Masking serious symptoms, drug resistance, adverse effects
med_danger_tr.keyFact: ⚠️ Paracetamol is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States, United Kingdom, and many developed countries — not because people intentionally overdose, but because doses are unknowingly accumulated from multiple sources.
details: Mechanism of liver toxicity (hepatotoxicity): at normal doses, paracetamol is safely glucuronidated and sulphated. With overdose, these pathways become saturated → CYP2E1 generates NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) — an extremely potent toxin. Glutathione used to neutralise NAPQI is rapidly depleted → NAPQI binds to liver proteins → hepatocyte necrosis.

Safe limits: healthy adults — maximum 4g/day (8 × 500mg tablets), evenly spaced every 6 hours. Regular drinkers — maximum 2g/day because CYP2E1 is already upregulated and glutathione depleted by alcohol. Liver disease, severe malnutrition, or prolonged fasting — also requires dose reduction.

Hidden danger: paracetamol is in hundreds of over-the-counter combination products — cold and flu tablets, cough syrups, combination sleep aids, prescription-strength pain relievers. Taking two Panadol tablets + one Decolgen sachet + one Efferalgan tablet may already be close to the 4g/day limit without realising it.

Stages of overdose symptoms: Stage 1 (0–24h): nausea, vomiting, fatigue — easily dismissed as normal. Stage 2 (24–72h): right upper abdominal pain, elevated liver enzymes. Stage 3 (72–96h): acute liver failure, jaundice, coagulopathy, possible death. Stage 4: recovery or death/liver transplant.

Narrow treatment window: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is an effective antidote if given within 8–10 hours of overdose — efficacy drops sharply after 24 hours. This is why you must go to A&E immediately when poisoning is suspected, without waiting for obvious symptoms.

Practical advice: always read the label of every medication you take and look for "paracetamol" or "acetaminophen" (the US name) or "APAP". If taking more than one paracetamol-containing product, add up the total dose. Do not drink alcohol within 24 hours before or after taking high-dose paracetamol.

points.label: NAPQI destroys liver cells — irreversibly
points.note: Glutathione depleted in 8–10 hours — treatment window is very narrow

points.label: Many drugs contain paracetamol
points.note: Decolgen + Panadol + Efferalgan = nearly the 4g/day limit

points.label: Drinkers: safe limit drops to 2g/day
points.note: CYP2E1 upregulated → more NAPQI, less glutathione

points.label: A&E within 8–10 hours — N-acetylcysteine
points.note: After 24h: NAC is much less effective — do not wait for symptoms

med_danger_tr.keyFact: 💊 Water-soluble vitamins (B, C) are excreted in urine if in excess — relatively safe at high doses. But fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate in fat tissue and the liver, causing toxicity with prolonged high-dose use.
details: Vitamin A (retinol) — the leading cause of birth defects: doses > 10,000 IU/day in pregnant women (especially the first trimester) increase the risk of heart defects, great vessel abnormalities, cleft lip/palate, and neural tube defects. Isotretinoin (Accutane, an acne drug) — a synthetic form of vitamin A — requires two forms of contraception due to its extremely high teratogenicity risk. In adults: acute toxicity (> 150,000 IU at once) causes nausea and headache; chronic toxicity (> 15,000 IU/day long-term) causes osteoporosis and liver damage.

Vitamin D — the most misused "wonder supplement": the WHO safe upper limit (UL) is 4,000 IU/day for adults. Many people self-administer 10,000–50,000 IU/day without monitoring levels. Hypervitaminosis D → hypercalcaemia → nausea, thirst, frequent urination, kidney stones, calcification of kidneys and blood vessels, cardiac arrhythmia. Measure 25(OH)D blood levels to determine the right dose.

High-dose vitamin E and coagulation: the HOPE-TOO study found vitamin E > 400 IU/day increases the risk of heart failure and all-cause mortality. Vitamin E inhibits platelet aggregation and interacts with warfarin → increased bleeding. Stop vitamin E > 400 IU at least 2 weeks before surgery.

Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) and peripheral neuropathy: this is a water-soluble vitamin but is still toxic at high doses. B6 > 500 mg/day long-term → peripheral neuropathy (numbness, pain, loss of sensation in hands and feet), possibly impairing the ability to walk. Nerve damage may be irreversible after stopping.

High-dose vitamin C (> 2g/day): less dangerous, but high doses increase urinary oxalate → kidney stones (especially in people with a history of stones). Can also cause excessive iron absorption in people with haemochromatosis. And "rebound scurvy": when stopped abruptly after prolonged high-dose use, the body continues rapid excretion → temporary vitamin C deficiency.

General principle: supplement vitamins only when there is evidence of deficiency (blood test) or increased need (pregnancy, malabsorption, highly restrictive diets). "Preventive" use at high doses without monitoring is unnecessary and potentially harmful. A varied diet is the best and safest source of vitamins.

points.label: Vitamin A > 10,000 IU → birth defects
points.note: Absolutely avoid high doses during or before pregnancy

points.label: Vitamin D: measure 25(OH)D before high-dose use
points.note: UL is 4,000 IU/day — do not self-increase to 10,000–50,000 IU

points.label: Vitamin E > 400 IU: increased bleeding, stop before surgery
points.note: Inhibits platelets + interacts with warfarin — stop 2 weeks before surgery

points.label: Vitamin B6 > 500 mg/day → limb numbness
points.note: Water-soluble but still toxic at high doses — nerve damage may be irreversible

med_danger_tr.keyFact: 📋 In most countries, dietary supplements do not need to prove efficacy before they are sold. Manufacturers are not required to report side effects. Regulatory bodies only intervene after problems arise.
details: Weak regulatory framework: in the US, the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA 1994) allows supplements to be sold without proving efficacy or safety before going to market — the complete opposite of drugs. In Vietnam, supplements are regulated as food, not drugs — significantly lower safety standards.

Heavy metal contamination: analysis of thousands of supplement samples (ConsumerLab, NSF, AOAC) found 20–30% containing lead, mercury, cadmium, or arsenic above safe levels. Highest risk: traditional Chinese and Indian medicine imports, botanical extracts from plants grown in polluted soil.

Undisclosed pharmaceutical ingredients: the FDA has found hundreds of supplement products containing unlisted pharmaceutical compounds — most commonly sildenafil/tadalafil in "male enhancement" products, sibutramine (a withdrawn weight-loss drug with cardiac risks) in diet products, anabolic steroids in muscle-building supplements, and corticosteroids in "herbal joint" preparations.

Real interactions with prescription drugs: fish oil > 3g/day + warfarin → increased bleeding; CoQ10 + warfarin → affects INR; calcium + levothyroxine → reduces thyroid hormone absorption; high-dose zinc → interferes with copper absorption → copper deficiency; iron + most antibiotics → reduced antibiotic absorption. Never regard supplements as "harmless with medications".

Reliable quality certification: look for independent third-party labels — NSF International, USP Verified, ConsumerLab, Informed-Sport. These certify that the product contains what the label says, is uncontaminated, and does not contain banned substances (important for athletes). This does NOT mean "effective" — only "clean".

Golden rule: always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all supplements you take, even "just a vitamin" or "natural herb". Especially important before surgery, when adjusting long-term medications, and during pregnancy. A doctor cannot help you if they do not have complete information.

points.label: Supplements do not require proven efficacy
points.note: FDA/Vietnam Ministry of Health: supplements sold without prior clinical trials

points.label: 20–30% of supplements contain excess heavy metals
points.note: Especially: traditional medicine imports from China and India

points.label: Hidden ingredients: sildenafil, steroids, sibutramine
points.note: FDA has found hundreds of "herbal" products containing real drugs

points.label: Look for NSF / USP Verified / ConsumerLab seal
points.note: Independent certification = clean product, correct ingredients (not = effective)

ml_filters_tr.title: Who created this content?
ml_filters_tr.sub: Qualified health professional, or anonymous account?
ml_filters_tr.keyFact: 🏛️ 97% of misleading health information spreading online originates from unverified sources. The credibility of the author and the organization behind the content is the fastest and most effective filter.
details: Source hierarchy: Tier 1 — international health organizations (WHO, CDC, NIH, EMA) and national ministries of health: issue guidelines based on synthesis of thousands of studies. Tier 2 — peer-reviewed journals (Nature Medicine, Lancet, NEJM, JAMA, BMJ): each article reviewed by at least 2–3 independent experts. Tier 3 — reputable hospitals and research centers: Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic, medical universities. Tier 4 and below: mass media (reporting on research — not the original research), blogs, social media.

Peer-review process: when a scientist submits a paper, the journal sends it to 2–3 independent experts in the field to evaluate methods, results, and conclusions. The process typically takes 3–12 months. Many papers are rejected (rejection rates at Lancet and NEJM exceed 90%). Peer-review is imperfect but is the most important filtering mechanism in science.

Predatory journals — the false prestige trap: there are thousands of "open" journals charging publication fees ($500–5,000 USD) but conducting no real peer-review — accepting nearly every submission. Beall's List catalogs predatory journals. Names sound scientific ("Journal of Advanced Medical Research") but carry no credibility. Verify a journal on PubMed or Scopus before trusting it.

Checking author and organization: does the author have relevant credentials and expertise (cardiologist writing about heart disease vs software engineer writing about cancer treatment)? Is the organization connected to a product being promoted? Does the article list a specific author (not just "Editorial Board")? Are any conflicts of interest declared?

Social media and echo chambers: Facebook, TikTok, YouTube use algorithms to keep users engaged — not to provide accurate information. Emotionally charged content (fear, outrage, miracle claims) spreads faster than accurate but dull information. MIT research (2018) found false news spreads 6 times faster than true news on Twitter. Facebook health groups have no mechanism for expert moderation.

Quick source-checking tools: Google Scholar (scholar.google.com) — find original scientific papers. PubMed (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) — the largest medical database. Snopes, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact — check misinformation. WHO Myth Busters — debunk common misconceptions. Full Fact (UK) — health fact-checking.

points.label: Peer-review = reviewed by experts
points.note: Lancet, NEJM reject >90% of submissions — only the best are published

points.label: Predatory journals: scientific name, no peer-review
points.note: Check on PubMed/Scopus before trusting a source

points.label: Social media: false news spreads 6× faster than truth
points.note: Algorithms prioritize engagement, not accuracy

points.label: Google Scholar + PubMed: find original studies
points.note: News articles report on research — they are not the research itself

ml_filters_tr.title: Where was it published?
ml_filters_tr.sub: Peer-reviewed journal, reputable media, or social media?
ml_filters_tr.keyFact: 🔬 The evidence pyramid: systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top, RCTs in the middle, and personal anecdotes at the bottom. "One person used it and recovered" is the weakest form of evidence — it cannot distinguish real effect from natural recovery or placebo.
details: The evidence pyramid (from strongest to weakest): (1) Systematic review + meta-analysis: synthesizes all RCTs on a question — highest accuracy. (2) RCT (Randomized Controlled Trial): random group assignment with a control group — the "gold standard" for proving causation. (3) Cohort study: follows a group of people over time. (4) Case-control: compares people with a disease to those without. (5) Case report: documents 1–few cases. (6) Expert opinion. (7) Anecdote (personal story).

Why a control group is necessary: suppose you take drug X and recover in 7 days — the drug may have worked, but the illness may have resolved naturally (common colds resolve in 5–10 days), or you changed your lifestyle simultaneously, or it was the placebo effect. Only an RCT with a control group (taking a placebo) can distinguish the true effect from these confounders.

Placebo effect — stronger than you think: research shows placebo can reduce pain by 30–40%, improve depression symptoms by 25–35%, and even reduce observable Parkinson's symptoms. This is why every drug must be compared to placebo in an RCT, not just "versus no treatment." The story "I used X and got better" cannot rule out placebo.

P-value and statistical significance — widely misunderstood: p < 0.05 means "the probability this result occurred by chance is less than 5%" — not "the drug is 95% effective." A small study (n=50) may yield p < 0.05 but have a tiny effect size (no clinical significance). Effect size must be examined alongside p-value. Statistical significance ≠ clinical significance.

Replication crisis — even published research can be wrong: the Reproducibility Project (2015) attempted to replicate 100 published psychology studies — only 36–39% produced similar results. In medicine, many initial "discoveries" from small studies fail to be confirmed in larger subsequent trials. This is why meta-analyses and systematic reviews matter more than any single study.

Signs of weak or biased research: small sample size (n < 100 with broad conclusions); no control group; self-reported outcomes (easily biased); short follow-up; animal studies extrapolated to humans; no disclosure of conflicts of interest; results too good to be true (unrealistically large effect size); published only once with no replication.

points.label: Systematic review > RCT > anecdote
points.note: Evidence pyramid — "one person recovered" sits at the bottom

points.label: Placebo reduces pain by 30–40% — cannot be ignored
points.note: Only an RCT with placebo can distinguish real from placebo effect

points.label: P-value ≠ actual effectiveness
points.note: p < 0.05 does not mean the drug works — check effect size too

points.label: Replication crisis: 39% of studies cannot be replicated
points.note: One study is not enough — look for a body of evidence

ml_filters_tr.title: Is research cited?
ml_filters_tr.sub: Does it reference real, peer-reviewed studies?
ml_filters_tr.keyFact: 🧠 Carl Sagan's principle: "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence." The more extreme the claim (cures everything, no side effects, 100% effective), the stronger the evidence required — and it is usually absent.
details: Language analysis — spotting inflated claims: CREDIBLE language: "may help improve," "according to study X conducted on population Y," "some people report," "research shows an association" (not causation). SUSPICIOUS language: "cures," "completely eliminates," "100%," "no side effects," "miracle," "breakthrough," "what doctors don't want you to know." Nothing in medicine is "100%" — even vaccines do not achieve 100% effectiveness in all individuals.

Biological plausibility: does the claim have a plausible physiological mechanism? Example: "vitamin C supports immunity" — clear mechanism (cofactor for collagen synthesis, supports immune cell function). In contrast: "alkaline water cures cancer" — no plausible mechanism (the stomach neutralizes pH immediately; water cannot change blood pH without severe alkalosis).

Dose-response relationship: a substance with a real biological effect typically exhibits dose-response — more leads to greater effect (up to a point). The absence of dose-response strongly suggests no real mechanism. The claim "just 1 drop per day cures all diseases" violates this principle.

The universality trap — nothing cures "all diseases": cancer is not one disease — it is over 200 distinct diseases with different mechanisms and treatments. A claim that one substance cures diabetes, cancer, and hypertension simultaneously is a clear red flag. Even aspirin, one of the most studied drugs in history, has specific indications — it is not "good for everything."

Conspiracy framing — "doctors are hiding this from you": the claim that mainstream medicine "conceals" cures to profit from sick patients misunderstands how science works. Millions of scientists, doctors, and researchers worldwide work independently — no global conspiracy can remain secret at that scale. If a real cancer cure existed, it would be the discovery of the century — whoever found it would be globally famous and wealthy, with no motive to hide it.

Checking consistency with established medical knowledge: if a claim contradicts thousands of replicated studies, it demands extraordinarily strong counter-evidence. The claim "no vaccine is safe" contradicts hundreds of millions of safety data points spanning decades. Scientific consensus can be wrong — but rarely — and it changes through evidence, not through viral posts.

points.label: "100% cure" = never true in medicine
points.note: Even vaccines don't achieve 100% in all people — nothing is absolute

points.label: No dose-response = high suspicion of no real effect
points.note: "1 drop cures all diseases" violates basic physiology principles

points.label: No global conspiracy hides a cancer cure
points.note: Millions of independent scientists cannot collectively keep one secret

points.label: Contradicts consensus = needs very strong evidence
points.note: Consensus changes through data, not through viral posts

ml_filters_tr.title: Is something being sold?
ml_filters_tr.sub: Supplements, courses, devices with extravagant promises?
ml_filters_tr.keyFact: 💰 Conflict of interest does not mean the information is wrong — but it is a reason to increase your skepticism. When the person sharing information stands to benefit financially if you believe them, ask harder questions.
details: Types of conflicts of interest (COI): Direct financial: selling products, affiliate commissions, funded by a related company.
