Indirect financial: research funded by an industry with a stake in the outcome (e.g., sugar research funded by a beverage company). Personal/reputational: celebrities wanting to maintain a "expert" image, KOLs wanting to grow their audience. All can unconsciously influence how information is presented.

Affiliate marketing in health content: many health bloggers, influencers, and podcasts earn 20–50% commission on products sold through their links. This creates a strong incentive to praise products — even without evidence. The FTC (US) requires disclosure of affiliate relationships, but many comply only minimally or not at all. Regulations in Vietnam on health affiliate disclosure are even looser.

Industry-funded research bias: analysis of hundreds of studies shows industry-funded research is 3–5 times more likely to produce results favorable to the funding industry than independent research. This is not always fraud — it may be publication bias (not publishing unfavorable results), selective reporting, or advantageous study design. Classic example: the Sugar Research Foundation's funding shifted blame for cardiovascular disease from sugar to fat in the 1960s–70s.

Paid and sponsored content: paid content is often designed to look like regular editorial content (native advertising). Look for labels like "Sponsored," "Advertorial," "#PR" — their absence is a red flag. Many Vietnamese health websites publish product PR articles without clearly marking them as advertisements.

Quick ways to detect conflicts of interest: are there purchase links or affiliate links at the end of the article? Does the author/website sell related products? Does the article disclose who funded the research (academic papers list "Funding" at the end)? Has this "KOL" been sponsored by pharma or supplement companies at conferences? Have they received free product samples?

Conflicts of interest exist in academia too: doctors and researchers may receive funding from pharmaceutical companies to speak at conferences, serve as advisors, or be named in studies. ProPublica's Dollars for Docs (US) allows lookup of payments from pharmaceutical companies to doctors. This does not automatically mean the doctor is wrong — but it is relevant context for objective evaluation. Many reputable journals require disclosure of all COIs.

points.label: Purchase link at end of article = financial motive
points.note: Affiliate commission 20–50%: strong incentive to praise products

points.label: Industry-funded research: 3–5× more favorable results
points.note: Check "Funding" section in research papers to see who paid

points.label: Look for "#ad", "sponsored", "funded" in content
points.note: No disclosure = increase skepticism about objectivity

points.label: COI ≠ wrong, but = requires more caution
points.note: Seek independent confirmation when you find a conflict of interest

ml_filters_tr.title: Is there a conflict of interest?
ml_filters_tr.sub: Sponsored? Financially benefits from the advice?
ml_filters_tr.keyFact: 📅 Medicine is not static — treatment guidelines are updated regularly as new evidence emerges. What was "correct" in 2010 may have been overturned by 2024. Checking the publication date is an important habit.
details: Medicine changes faster than you think: more than 1 million new medical papers are published every year. Clinical guidelines from AHA, ADA, ESC, and WHO are typically updated every 3–5 years. In fields like oncology and infectious disease, guidelines can change within months when new evidence emerges.

Major instances where medicine reversed its position: Dietary fat and heart disease (1960–1990 vs 2010–present): old guidelines said "reduce fat to protect the heart" → today: moderate saturated fat is safer than refined carbohydrates. Eggs and cholesterol (1970–2010 vs 2015–present): "no more than 1 egg per day" → FDA 2015 no longer limits dietary cholesterol. HRT (hormone replacement therapy) and breast cancer: WHO's Women's Health Initiative (2002) caused alarm → reanalysis showed risk depends on HRT type, age at initiation, and duration of use.

Aspirin and cardiovascular prevention — an important reversal: for decades, low-dose aspirin was recommended for everyone over 50 to prevent cardiovascular events. The ASPREE (2018) and ARRIVE (2018) trials showed healthy individuals without prior cardiovascular disease benefit little and face increased bleeding risk. AHA/ACC (2019) reversed the recommendation: aspirin is no longer recommended for people over 70 or those at low risk. An article from 2015 about aspirin may lead to incorrect practice today.

Living guidelines and continuous updates: some organizations such as WHO, NICE (UK), and many specialty societies provide "living guidelines" — updated continuously as new evidence emerges, rather than waiting for periodic revision cycles. COVID-19 was the clearest example: guidelines changed weekly in the early pandemic. This is how science should work — not a sign that science is "unreliable."

Checking article publication and last-updated dates: many websites do not display publication dates, or show a date without a last-updated date. Google date trick: search using Google and look below the URL for the indexing date. Facebook timestamp trick: click the timestamp (e.g., "3 hours ago") to see the exact posting date. For Wikipedia: see "Last edited" at the bottom and check the edit history.

Old articles spreading as new — a serious problem: social media allows resharing of old content without modification — a 2012 article can go viral in 2024 with sharers unaware it is outdated. Some health blogs deliberately do not show dates — a transparency red flag. Practical tip: search "site:pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov [topic] [recent year]" to find the latest research.

points.label: Aspirin 2015 vs 2019: recommendation fully reversed
points.note: A 2015 article may recommend aspirin that AHA 2019 has withdrawn

points.label: Eggs, fat, HRT: all have changed positions
points.note: Medicine is not wrong — it updates when better evidence arrives

points.label: 2012 article viral in 2024 — no one flags it
points.note: Click Facebook timestamp to see the actual posting date

points.label: PubMed: filter by most recent 3–5 years
points.note: A new systematic review outranks any blog post

prev_vaccines_tr.keyFact: 🤧 The flu virus mutates every year — last year's vaccine does not protect you this year. WHO monitors circulating influenza strains globally and updates the vaccine formula twice a year. Annual flu vaccination reduces the risk of flu by 40–60% and significantly reduces the risk of severe complications.
details: Why you need a new flu vaccine every year: unlike measles or hepatitis B vaccines that provide lifelong immunity, influenza A and B viruses mutate at an extremely high rate — particularly the surface proteins H (hemagglutinin) and N (neuraminidase). Each season, new strains become dominant. WHO operates a network of 150 surveillance centers in 114 countries to predict which strains will circulate and updates the vaccine formula twice per year (for the Northern and Southern hemispheres).

Real-world effectiveness and who benefits most: flu vaccine effectiveness ranges from 40–60% depending on the year (how well the vaccine matches circulating strains). This may sound low, but even when not a perfect match, the vaccine reduces disease severity, hospitalizations, and deaths. Those who benefit most: people ≥ 65 years (highest complication risk), pregnant women (protects both mother and baby), children 6 months – 5 years, people with chronic conditions (heart, lung, diabetes), and healthcare workers.

Optimal timing in Vietnam: Vietnam's flu season varies by region — the North peaks in winter (November–March), the South peaks around the rainy season (May–October). Vaccinate 2–4 weeks before flu season to allow sufficient antibody development. Practically speaking, you can be vaccinated any time of year — later is still better than never. Immunity peaks after 2 weeks and lasts approximately 6–12 months.

Flu complications — not just a "bad cold": influenza can cause primary viral pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia, myocarditis, encephalitis, and multi-organ failure. Global flu deaths: 290,000–650,000 per year (WHO). The particularly severe 2017–2018 US flu season resulted in 810,000 hospitalizations and 61,000 deaths. Children under 5 and adults over 65 account for the majority of deaths.

Herd immunity and community protection: when flu vaccination rates in a community exceed 60–70%, even those who cannot be vaccinated (infants < 6 months, those with severe allergies) are indirectly protected because the virus has fewer hosts to spread through. Getting vaccinated protects not just yourself — it protects grandparents, young children, and vulnerable people around you. This is why healthcare workers are often mandated to receive annual flu vaccination in many countries.

Quadrivalent flu vaccines — the modern choice: older flu vaccines protected only against 3 strains (trivalent). Quadrivalent vaccines protect against 4 strains: 2 influenza A (H1N1 and H3N2) + 2 influenza B. WHO now recommends quadrivalent vaccines. In Vietnam, quadrivalent flu vaccines are available at major vaccination centers (VNVC, Safpo). Cost approximately 200,000–350,000 VND — a small investment compared to treating complicated flu.

points.label: Virus mutates yearly — last year's vaccine is no longer effective
points.note: WHO updates the formula twice a year based on surveillance in 114 countries

points.label: ≥ 65, pregnant, chronic illness: annual vaccination priority
points.note: Even 40–60% effectiveness significantly reduces severe complications and deaths

points.label: VN: vaccinate before winter (North) or rainy season (South)
points.note: Later is still better than never — immunity peaks in 2 weeks

points.label: Choose quadrivalent — protects against 4 strains instead of 3
points.note: Available at VNVC, Safpo — approximately 200–350k VND/dose

prev_vaccines_tr.keyFact: 🦠 The COVID-19 situation continues to evolve — vaccine recommendations are updated based on community immunity levels, circulating strains, and new evidence. General principle: high-risk individuals (≥ 60 years, chronic conditions, immunocompromised) benefit most from periodic booster doses.
details: mRNA technology — a vaccine revolution: Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna vaccines use mRNA technology — the first time this technology was deployed at scale. mRNA never enters the cell nucleus and does not interact with DNA. Cells read the mRNA to produce the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies and memory T/B cells. mRNA is completely degraded within a few days — it does not persist long-term in the body.

Effectiveness over time and why boosters are needed: immunity from both vaccination and natural infection wanes over time, especially against new variants. Neutralizing antibodies decline fastest (within months), but memory T and B cells are more durable — this is why vaccines continue to protect against severe disease even as measurable antibodies decrease. Booster doses "reawaken" the immune system, boosting both antibodies and memory cells, and are updated to match circulating strains (like flu vaccines).

Those who benefit most from boosters: people ≥ 60 years (highest risk of severe COVID, natural immune decline with age). Immunocompromised (organ transplants, chemotherapy, uncontrolled HIV). Severe chronic conditions (COPD, diabetes, heart failure). Healthcare workers (high exposure, protecting vulnerable patients). In Vietnam: follow guidance from the Ministry of Health — updated at moh.gov.vn.

Long COVID — another reason to prevent infection: approximately 10–30% of COVID-19 patients (including mild cases) have symptoms persisting > 12 weeks after infection — called Long COVID or Post-COVID Condition. Common symptoms: chronic fatigue, difficulty concentrating ("brain fog"), shortness of breath, joint pain. Mechanisms being researched: chronic inflammation, autoimmune dysregulation, and microvascular damage. Vaccination reduces Long COVID risk by approximately 50% according to several studies.

Safety and side effects: common side effects (short-term, self-resolving): injection site pain (70–80%), fatigue (60%), headache (55%), chills (40%). Myocarditis (heart inflammation) after mRNA vaccines: rare, primarily in males aged 16–29 after dose 2. Rate: approximately 12–40 cases per million doses — and most resolve within a few days. Importantly: the risk of myocarditis from actual COVID-19 infection is many times higher than from vaccination. Over 13 billion doses administered globally — short-to-medium-term safety profile is closely monitored.

Why you cannot rely solely on "natural immunity": post-infection immunity is uneven — those with severe illness generally develop stronger immunity than those with mild illness. Allowing oneself to get COVID for the purpose of immunity carries unacceptable risks (death, Long COVID, risk to vulnerable contacts). Hybrid immunity (infection + vaccination) often provides broader and more durable immunity than either alone. Most of the population now has some level of hybrid immunity — periodic boosters help maintain protection.

points.label: mRNA does not enter the nucleus and does not interact with DNA
points.note: Completely degraded within days — breakthrough technology, safe in short-to-medium term

points.label: Antibodies decline after months — T/B memory cells are more durable
points.note: Vaccines continue to protect against severe disease even as measurable antibodies fall

points.label: Long COVID: 10–30% of mild cases have symptoms > 12 weeks
points.note: Vaccination reduces Long COVID risk ~50% — an additional reason to prevent infection

points.label: ≥ 60 + chronic conditions: prioritize boosters per MoH guidance
points.note: Follow moh.gov.vn for the latest recommendations for Vietnam

prev_vaccines_tr.keyFact: 🔬 Immunity from childhood Tdap vaccination wanes over time — many adults are no longer fully protected. Whooping cough (pertussis) is re-emerging in adults in many countries. Tetanus can be fatal — and the bacteria exist throughout the soil and environment.
details: Three diseases in one vaccine: Diphtheria: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces a toxin that causes a false membrane in the throat → airway obstruction, myocarditis, nerve paralysis. Case fatality rate 5–10%, higher in children. Vietnam had a diphtheria outbreak in mountainous regions in 2020 due to low vaccination rates. Tetanus: Clostridium tetani in soil, dust, feces → enters through wounds → severe muscle spasms → fatality rate 10–80% depending on severity. Pertussis (whooping cough): Bordetella pertussis → paroxysmal coughing lasting 100 days ("hundred-day cough"), most dangerous for infants < 6 months.

Why adults need boosters: childhood vaccination (DTaP) is typically completed at 4–6 years. Diphtheria and pertussis immunity wanes after 5–10 years. Tetanus immunity lasts longer (~10 years) but still requires boosting. CDC and WHO recommendations: one Tdap booster for adults who have not yet received Tdap (if previously only received Td). Thereafter: Td booster (without pertussis component) every 10 years. Special case: pregnant women should receive Tdap during each pregnancy (weeks 27–36).

Pertussis re-emerging — not just a childhood disease: many large pertussis outbreaks in recent years (US 2012: 48,277 cases — highest since 1955) occurred mainly in adolescents and adults. Adults without up-to-date boosters can carry the bacteria without classic symptoms (only persistent cough for a few weeks), then transmit to infants < 6 months who have not yet completed vaccination — the most vulnerable group (> 90% of pertussis deaths occur in infants < 6 months). Cocooning strategy: give Tdap to parents, siblings, and grandparents before the baby is born.

Tetanus — an ever-present risk: Clostridium tetani spores persist in soil, animal feces, and road dust — they cannot be completely avoided. Any wound (rusty nail, deep cut, burn, animal bite) can be an entry point. Symptoms appear 3–21 days after infection: jaw stiffness (lockjaw), generalized spasms, autonomic nervous system dysfunction. There is no specific treatment — only supportive care (ICU, ventilator). Fatality rates in developing countries still reach 50–80%.

Tetanus booster after injury: for high-risk wounds (deep, dirty, contaminated with soil/feces): booster is needed if not vaccinated within the past 5 years (not the usual 10 years). If vaccination history is unclear or incomplete: full 3-dose series (0, 1 month, 6–12 months). Tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG): given simultaneously with the vaccine for severe wounds in incompletely vaccinated individuals — provides immediate passive immunity while the vaccine generates active immunity.

Pregnant women — Tdap every pregnancy: CDC and WHO recommend Tdap at weeks 27–36 of every pregnancy (not only the first). Rationale: maternal antibodies cross the placenta — protecting the baby from birth until it is old enough for vaccination (2 months). Studies show up to 93% effectiveness in protecting newborns when the mother received Tdap during pregnancy. Safety: Tdap has been demonstrated safe in pregnancy across multiple large studies.

points.label: Booster every 10 years — childhood immunity wanes with age
points.note: High-risk wound: booster needed if not vaccinated within 5 years (not 10)

points.label: Whooping cough: asymptomatic adults transmit to infants < 6 months
points.note: Cocooning: vaccinate parents and grandparents before baby is born

points.label: Tetanus in soil and dust — unavoidable, fatality up to 50–80%
points.note: No specific treatment — only vaccination is effective prevention

points.label: Pregnancy: Tdap at weeks 27–36 each pregnancy — protects baby from birth
points.note: Maternal antibodies cross placenta — up to 93% protection for newborns

prev_vaccines_tr.keyFact: 🫀 Vietnam is a highly endemic region for hepatitis B — the HBsAg carrier rate in the population is 8–10%. Chronic hepatitis B is the leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in Vietnam. The hepatitis B vaccine is > 95% effective and provides lifelong immunity in those who complete the 3-dose series.
details: Hepatitis B in Vietnam — the true burden: Vietnam has approximately 8–10 million people chronically infected with HBV (HBsAg positive). Liver cancer is the 2nd most common cancer and the leading cause of cancer death in Vietnamese men — 75–80% are due to HBV. Hepatitis B is transmitted via: blood (transfusions, shared needles, tattooing, acupuncture with non-sterile equipment), sexual contact, and vertical transmission from mother to child (the primary route in Vietnam).

How it spreads — and how it does not: DOES spread via: blood and body fluids (semen, vaginal secretions, breast milk), mother to child (perinatal), sharing razors, toothbrushes, or needles. DOES NOT spread via: handshakes, hugs, cheek kisses, sharing food, coughing, sneezing, or swimming pools. HBV is present in blood at 50–100 times higher concentrations than HIV — it can transmit through very small blood exposures. Nail salon tools, tattoo equipment, and non-sterile acupuncture needles are important transmission sources to be aware of.

Vaccination schedule — 3 primary doses and immunity check: standard schedule: dose 1 (month 0) → dose 2 (month 1) → dose 3 (month 6). Accelerated schedule: 0–1–2 months + dose 4 at 12 months (used when rapid protection is needed, e.g., before travel). After completing 3 doses: check Anti-HBs (protective antibody titer) 1–2 months later. Anti-HBs ≥ 10 mIU/mL = protected. Anti-HBs < 10 mIU/mL = "non-responder" (approximately 5–10% of adults) — need 3 more doses and recheck.

Pre-vaccination testing: test for HBsAg (currently infected?), Anti-HBs (already immune?), and Anti-HBc (past HBV exposure?). If HBsAg positive: do not vaccinate — treat HBV instead. If Anti-HBs positive (≥ 10 mIU/mL): already immune, no vaccine needed. If both negative: not immune, vaccinate promptly. In Vietnam, many people are either chronically infected (8–10%) or already immune from childhood vaccination — testing before vaccination avoids unnecessary doses.

Protecting newborns — first dose within 24 hours: newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers have a 70–90% chance of HBV infection without intervention. Current protocol: hepatitis B vaccine within 12–24 hours of birth + HBIG (hepatitis B immune globulin) — reduces infection risk to < 5–10%. This is why the hepatitis B vaccine has been included in Vietnam's national immunization program since 1997, with the first dose within 24 hours. For newborns of mothers with unknown HBsAg status: test the mother immediately and vaccinate as early as possible.

Adults who should prioritize vaccination: healthcare workers (high blood exposure). People with multiple sexual partners or men who have sex with men. People who inject drugs. People living with or having sexual contact with HBsAg-positive individuals. Patients with chronic kidney disease/dialysis (often need higher doses). Travelers to high-endemicity regions. And in practice: all adults without immunity should be vaccinated — the vaccine is safe, effective, and provides lifelong protection.

points.label: VN: 8–10 million with HBV — liver cancer the leading cancer in men
points.note: Mother-to-child transmission is the primary route — first dose within 24h of birth

points.label: Test for HBsAg + Anti-HBs before vaccination
points.note: Already immune or currently infected: do not need / should not receive vaccine

points.label: Anti-HBs ≥ 10 mIU/mL after 3 doses = lifelong protection
points.note: 5–10% are non-responders — check after 1–2 months, revaccinate if needed

points.label: Nail salon tools, tattoo needles, acupuncture — transmission risk
points.note: HBV in blood is 50–100× more concentrated than HIV — even small exposure can infect

prev_vaccines_tr.keyFact: 🎗️ The HPV vaccine is the first and only vaccine proven to PREVENT CANCER — not just prevent infection. HPV causes 99% of cervical cancers, 90% of anal cancers, and 70% of oropharyngeal cancers. Vaccine effectiveness reaches 97–99% against high-risk HPV strains when administered before exposure.
details: What is HPV and why is it so common: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is a virus transmitted through skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity — including vaginal, anal, and oral sex. An estimated 80–90% of sexually active people will acquire at least one HPV strain during their lifetime. Most infections clear spontaneously within 1–2 years through immune response. The problem: certain strains (particularly HPV-16 and HPV-18) persist long-term → integrate into cell DNA → cause malignant transformation. There are no symptoms during infection — a person does not know they are carrying the virus.

Diseases caused by HPV: Cervical cancer (CC): 99% caused by HPV — HPV-16 and HPV-18 account for 70% of cases. Anal cancer: 90% caused by HPV. Vulvar, vaginal, penile cancers: 40–90% caused by HPV. Oropharyngeal cancer (mouth/throat): HPV-16 causes 70–80% of cases, with rapidly increasing incidence in men. Genital warts (condyloma): caused by HPV-6 and HPV-11 (low-risk strains). Gardasil 9 protects against 9 strains: HPV-6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 — covering approximately 90% of cervical cancers.

Vaccination schedule by age: 9–14 years (before exposure): 2 doses (0 and 6–12 months) — the immune system at this age responds more robustly, so 2 doses provide equivalent immunity to 3 doses in adults. 15–45 years: 3 doses (0, 2, and 6 months). Over 45: FDA (US) extended approval to age 45, but benefit decreases as likelihood of prior HPV exposure increases — consult a doctor. Key point: vaccine is most effective BEFORE exposure — but still beneficial for sexually active individuals who may not have encountered all strains.

Should men get the HPV vaccine: Yes, absolutely. Men are also affected by anal cancer, penile cancer, and oropharyngeal cancer due to HPV. HPV-16-related throat cancer in men is increasing rapidly in the US and Europe. Genital warts (HPV-6/11): cause significant discomfort and costly treatment. Vaccinating men also reduces HPV transmission to sexual partners. CDC recommends HPV vaccine for everyone through age 26 regardless of gender, and considers it through age 45.

Real-world effectiveness after mass deployment: Australia launched its national HPV vaccination program in 2007 for girls and 2013 for boys. Results by 2023: cervical cancer in women under 30 decreased by > 90% — approaching the goal of cervical cancer elimination. Scotland: 89% reduction in cervical cancer rates among women vaccinated at age 12–13. This is the strongest real-world evidence: vaccination works not just in clinical trials but in actual populations.

HPV vaccine and cervical cancer screening: the vaccine does not replace screening (Pap smear / HPV test). Reason: vaccine protects against ~90% of strains, not 100%. Vaccinated individuals still need regular screening. Current screening guidelines: Pap smear every 3 years (from age 21), or HPV test + Pap smear (co-test) every 5 years (from age 30), or HPV test alone every 5 years (from age 25). In Vietnam: HPV testing is increasingly available at major hospitals.

points.label: First vaccine proven to PREVENT CANCER — not just infection
points.note: Gardasil 9 covers 9 HPV strains — includes ~90% of cervical cancer strains

points.label: Men should get vaccinated — HPV-16 throat cancer rising fast
points.note: CDC recommends for everyone through age 26, consider through age 45

points.label: Australia: cervical cancer reduced > 90% in vaccinated generation
points.note: Real-world population evidence — cervical cancer elimination is achievable

points.label: Vaccine does not replace Pap smear / HPV test screening
points.note: Screening every 3–5 years still necessary — 90% protection is not 100%

prev_vaccines_tr.keyFact: 🫁 Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the leading cause of bacterial pneumonia, meningitis, and sepsis in older adults. In countries with national pneumococcal vaccination programs, rates of severe pneumonia and death in individuals ≥ 65 years have decreased by 50–80%.
details: Streptococcus pneumoniae — the most dangerous opportunistic pathogen: pneumococcus is a bacterium that normally colonizes the nose and throat of 5–40% of healthy individuals (higher in children and the elderly). Most of the time it causes no illness — but when the immune system is weakened (by flu, COVID, aging, or chronic illness): it invades the lungs, bloodstream, or meninges. There are over 90 serotypes (strains) of pneumococcus — vaccines protect against the serotypes responsible for the most severe disease.

Diseases caused by pneumococcus: Bacterial pneumonia (pneumococcal pneumonia): high fever, productive cough, shortness of breath — may require hospitalization or ICU. Fatality rate in the elderly: 20–30%. Bacterial meningitis: fever, stiff neck, light sensitivity — fatality rate 20–30%, severe neurological sequelae (deafness, paralysis) in survivors. Bacteremia/sepsis: bacteria enter the bloodstream — high mortality especially in the elderly and immunocompromised.

Two types of pneumococcal vaccines — PCV and PPSV: PPSV23 (Pneumovax): polysaccharide vaccine covering 23 serotypes. Provides only short-term immunity (5–7 years), does not generate B-cell memory, poorly effective in children < 2 years. PCV13 (Prevenar 13) / PCV15 / PCV20: conjugate vaccine — protein attached to polysaccharide → activates T + B memory cells → more durable, more effective immunity. PCV20 (Prevnar 20) covers 20 serotypes — gradually replacing PCV13. Current recommendations: PCV20 or PCV15 + PPSV23.

Who should be vaccinated and when: ≥ 65 years: PCV20 (1 dose) or PCV15 followed by PPSV23 (≥ 1 year later). Ages 19–64 with high risk: chronic lung disease (COPD, asthma), cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, asplenia, HIV, or immunosuppression. Smoking is also a risk factor (damages respiratory mucosa). Children < 5 years: PCV is part of the national immunization schedule — protecting children and reducing community spread (herd protection for the elderly).

Real-world vaccine effectiveness: after the US introduced PCV13 for adults in 2014: vaccine-strain pneumococcal pneumonia in people ≥ 65 years declined by 91–93% within a few years. Rates of bacteremia and pneumococcal meningitis fell significantly. Childhood PCV also creates indirect herd protection for the elderly: children carry fewer bacteria → less transmission to grandparents. This is an important example of the community-wide benefits of vaccination.

Distinguishing viral from bacterial pneumonia: viral pneumonia (including COVID, flu): does not respond to antibiotics, managed with supportive care. Pneumococcal pneumonia (bacterial): requires antibiotics (amoxicillin/clavulanate, azithromycin, fluoroquinolone). Antibiotic resistance: S. pneumoniae is increasingly resistant to penicillin and macrolides — an additional reason to prevent infection through vaccination rather than relying solely on antibiotic treatment. In Vietnam, antibiotic resistance in pneumococcus is high.

points.label: ≥ 65: pneumococcal pneumonia fatality 20–30% — 1 dose PCV20
points.note: Lung disease, cardiovascular disease, diabetes ages 19–64: also recommended

points.label: Pneumococcus increasingly resistant to antibiotics — prevent better than treat
points.note: High penicillin and macrolide resistance in VN — vaccination is the most effective defense

points.label: Children vaccinated with PCV reduce pneumococcal spread to grandparents
points.note: PCV in Vietnam's national schedule protects both children and the elderly community

points.label: PCV20: 1 dose covers 20 serotypes — replaces old 2-vaccine regimen
points.note: Prevnar 20 simplifies the schedule compared to previous PCV15 + PPSV23

prev_cancer_tr.title: Colorectal Cancer
prev_cancer_tr.keyFact: 🔭 Colorectal cancer (colon and rectal cancer) is the 3rd most common cancer worldwide — but the best PREVENTABLE cancer through screening. Colonoscopy does not just detect cancer early — it removes pre-cancerous polyps immediately during the same procedure, breaking the chain of progression to cancer.
details: Why colorectal cancer is uniquely preventable: the journey from polyp to cancer takes 10–15 years — the longest window of opportunity among all cancer types. Adenomatous polyps are the primary precursors: initially benign, gradually accumulating genetic mutations (APC, KRAS, TP53) → invasive cancer. Colonoscopy detects AND removes polyps immediately (polypectomy) → breaks the progression chain. This is why colorectal cancer screening can PREVENT cancer — not just detect it early.

Screening methods compared: Colonoscopy: the gold standard — visualizes the entire colon, removes polyps immediately. Every 10 years if results are normal. FIT (Fecal Immunochemical Test): non-invasive, performed at home, annually. If positive → colonoscopy needed to confirm. Sensitivity 60–80% for cancer. CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy): non-invasive, every 5 years. Cannot remove polyps. Flexible sigmoidoscopy: only views the end portion of the colon, every 5 years.

Who should start screening before age 45: high-risk individuals should begin at age 40 (or earlier): personal history of polyps or colorectal cancer. First-degree relatives (parents, siblings) with colorectal cancer — start screening 10 years earlier than the relative's age at diagnosis, or at age 40, whichever comes first. Hereditary syndromes: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) — start screening at 20–25 years, every 1–2 years. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) — may require prophylactic total colectomy.

Preparing for colonoscopy — what many people dread: bowel preparation is the most uncomfortable part: drinking a bowel cleansing solution (polyethylene glycol) the evening before. The colonoscopy procedure itself: typically 20–30 minutes, with light sedation — most patients do not remember the procedure. Recovery: go home the same day, may experience mild bloating. Rate of serious complications (perforation, bleeding): < 0.3% — very low for an invasive procedure. The discomfort of preparation is far less than the benefit of early cancer detection.

Risk factors for colorectal cancer: diet high in red/processed meat and low in fiber. Obesity (BMI > 30) — increases risk by 30–40%. Physical inactivity. Smoking. Alcohol consumption. Type 2 diabetes. Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis). Combination of multiple risk factors: individuals with 3+ risk factors may consider starting screening before age 45. Low-dose aspirin has evidence for reducing polyp recurrence — but discuss benefit/bleeding risk with a doctor.

Situation in Vietnam: colorectal cancer rates in Vietnam are rising rapidly — estimated increase of 3–4% per year, reflecting lifestyle changes (more red meat, less vegetables, less exercise, rising obesity). Colorectal cancer screening is not yet widespread in Vietnam — most cases are diagnosed at late stages (III–IV). Colonoscopy is available at major hospitals: Hanoi Medical University Hospital, Bach Mai Hospital, Cho Ray Hospital, Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital. Cost approximately 500,000–1,500,000 VND depending on the facility.

points.label: Colonoscopy = detect AND remove polyps — prevents cancer
points.note: Polyp to cancer takes 10–15 years — the longest prevention window

points.label: Annual at-home FIT test: alternative if you prefer no colonoscopy
points.note: If FIT positive → colonoscopy immediately, do not delay

points.label: First-degree relative with colorectal cancer: start 10 years earlier
points.note: Lynch syndrome: screening from age 20–25, every 1–2 years

points.label: Red/processed meat + low fiber + obesity: high-risk group
points.note: VN: rising 3–4%/year — most cases diagnosed at late stage

prev_cancer_tr.title: Breast Cancer
prev_cancer_tr.keyFact: 🎗️ Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women worldwide. Detected at Stage I (tumor < 2cm, no lymph node spread): 5-year survival > 99%. Detected at Stage IV (metastatic): 5-year survival only 28%. Regular mammography is the only tool proven to reduce breast cancer mortality in average-risk women.
details: Mammography — why it is the gold standard: a mammogram (low-dose breast X-ray) can detect tumors as small as 2–3mm — far smaller than the threshold detectable by touch (usually > 1–2cm). Early detection at this stage typically does not require chemotherapy and involves less radical surgery. Digital breast tomosynthesis (3D mammography): an improvement over 2D mammography — reduces recall rates and increases detection of invasive cancer, especially in women with dense breast tissue. Gradually replacing 2D mammography at major centers.

Debate about the starting age — why guidelines differ: USPSTF (2024): recommends starting at age 40 (updated from age 50 in 2016). ACS: starting at age 40 (optional), age 45 (strong recommendation). The difference reflects a trade-off: starting earlier (age 40) → earlier detection AND more false positives (causing anxiety and unnecessary biopsies). The final decision depends on individual risk and patient preference after discussion with a doctor.

High-risk women — enhanced screening: lifetime risk > 20%: annual breast MRI in addition to mammography. High-risk groups: BRCA1/BRCA2 gene mutation (lifetime breast cancer risk 50–85%), history of chest radiation (e.g., Hodgkin lymphoma treatment), strong family history (mother/sister with breast cancer < 50 years old). BRCA genetic testing: consider if ≥ 2 first-degree relatives have breast cancer or 1 relative has both breast and ovarian cancer. In Vietnam: BRCA testing available at Vinmec, Oncology Hospitals.

Breast density — a lesser-known factor: women with dense breast tissue (approximately 40% of women): mammography is less sensitive (cancer can be "hidden" in dense tissue), AND dense breast tissue is itself an independent risk factor. Women with dense breasts may benefit from: supplemental annual breast ultrasound (detects an additional 2–4 cancers per 1,000 women), or breast MRI if high-risk. Mammography results will indicate breast density (BI-RADS density A–D).

Breast self-examination — its proper role: monthly breast self-examination has NOT been proven to reduce breast cancer mortality in large RCTs. However: approximately 30–40% of breast cancers are discovered by the patient through sensing changes. Current recommendation: "breast awareness" — know what your breasts normally feel like and report any changes immediately (lump, orange-peel skin, nipple retraction, abnormal discharge). No need to follow a rigid self-examination routine — just be aware and report changes.

Breast cancer screening in Vietnam: breast cancer is the most common cancer in Vietnamese women (21.5% of all female cancers). Average age at diagnosis in Vietnam is lower than Western countries (40–50 vs 60–65). Late-stage detection rates in Vietnam remain high — largely because of insufficient routine screening. Mammography available at major hospitals: K Hospital Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital, Vinmec, major private hospitals. Mammogram cost: 300,000–800,000 VND. Breast ultrasound (supplemental or for younger/dense breast women): 150,000–400,000 VND.

points.label: Stage I: > 99% survival. Stage IV: only 28% — early detection = survival
points.note: Mammogram detects tumors from 2–3mm — far smaller than detectable by touch

points.label: BRCA1/BRCA2: lifetime breast cancer risk 50–85%
points.note: Genetic testing if ≥ 2 close relatives have breast cancer — available at Vinmec

points.label: Dense breast tissue (40% of women): mammogram less sensitive, add ultrasound
points.note: BI-RADS density C–D on mammogram report = dense breast tissue

points.label: VN: women get breast cancer younger than global average — screen from age 40
points.note: 21.5% of female cancers in VN — most detected late because of insufficient screening

prev_cancer_tr.title: Cervical Cancer
prev_cancer_tr.schedule: Pap smear every 3 years (from age 21) or HPV test every 5 years (from age 25)
prev_cancer_tr.keyFact: 🔬 Cervical cancer is a FULLY ELIMINABLE cancer — through the combination of HPV vaccination (preventing infection) and regular screening (detecting pre-cancerous lesions). Treatment of pre-cancer (CIN 2–3) achieves > 95% cure. Stage IV invasive cervical cancer: 5-year survival only 17%.
details: The journey from HPV to pre-cancer to cancer: high-risk HPV infection (mainly HPV-16/18) → cervical cells begin to change abnormally. CIN 1 (mild lesion): 60–80% resolve spontaneously. CIN 2 (moderate): 40–50% resolve, 20% progress. CIN 3 (severe, pre-cancer): less likely to resolve spontaneously, 12–30% progress to invasive cancer within 10 years if untreated. The entire journey from HPV infection to invasive cancer averages 10–20 years — regular screening provides ample time to detect and intervene.

Pap smear vs HPV test — the difference: Pap smear (cytology): collects cervical cells for microscopic examination to detect abnormal cells. Sensitivity 55–80% for CIN 2+. Every 3 years. HPV test: detects high-risk HPV DNA in cervical cells. Sensitivity > 95% for CIN 2+. Every 5 years. Co-test (Pap smear + HPV test simultaneously): highest sensitivity, every 5 years. Current trend: transitioning to HPV-only testing or co-testing instead of Pap-only — due to higher sensitivity and longer interval.

Reading Pap smear and HPV test results: Normal Pap smear: repeat on schedule. ASC-US (Atypical Squamous Cells of Undetermined Significance): reflex HPV test — if HPV negative: return to normal screening; if HPV positive: colposcopy. LSIL (Low-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion = CIN 1): typically monitored. HSIL (High-grade = CIN 2–3): colposcopy and biopsy → treatment. HPV positive (without abnormal cytology): retest after 1 year or proceed to colposcopy depending on strain (HPV-16/18 vs other strains).

Treatment of pre-cancer — a simple, highly effective intervention: CIN 2–3 is treated with: LEEP (Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure) — excision of cervical tissue with an electrosurgical wire loop under local anesthesia, 10–15 minutes, performed as an outpatient procedure. Success rate > 90–95%. Cryotherapy (cold treatment): only for small lesions, less commonly used. Conization (cone biopsy): removes a larger portion, used when invasion is suspected. After treatment: close monitoring with HPV test + Pap smear every 6–12 months × 3 years.

Why screening can stop after age 65: women 65+ with a history of adequate screening and normal results (3 consecutive negative Pap smears or 2 negative co-tests within the past 10 years, with the most recent within 5 years) may discontinue screening — the risk of developing cervical cancer afterwards is very low. DOES NOT APPLY to: women with a history of CIN 2+ (monitoring needed for 20–25 years post-treatment), immunosuppression, or inadequate prior screening history.

Cervical cancer screening in Vietnam: cervical cancer is the 2nd most common cancer in Vietnamese women (after breast cancer). Screening rates remain low, especially in rural areas. Screening is available at most obstetrics/gynecology hospitals: Tu Du Hospital, Hanoi Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital, general hospitals. Cost for Pap smear: 100,000–300,000 VND. HPV test: 500,000–1,000,000 VND. Free/low-cost screening programs: some provinces have community screening programs — check with the local health station.

points.label: HPV test every 5 years: > 95% sensitivity for CIN 2+ — better than Pap
points.note: Co-test (Pap + HPV): highest sensitivity, 5-year interval instead of 3 years

points.label: LEEP for CIN 2–3: 10–15 min, outpatient, > 95% effective
points.note: Pre-cancer treated simply → invasive cancer requires major surgery

points.label: Stop screening after age 65 if history is normal for ≥ 10 years
points.note: Does not apply with prior CIN 2+ history — monitoring for 20–25 more years

points.label: HPV vaccine + regular screening = can eliminate cervical cancer
points.note: Australia has achieved > 90% reduction in cervical cancer in vaccinated generation

prev_cancer_tr.title: Lung Cancer
prev_cancer_tr.schedule: Annual low-dose CT scan (ages 50–80 with ≥ 20 pack-years)
prev_cancer_tr.keyFact: 🫁 Lung cancer kills more people than breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers combined. 85% of cases are diagnosed at advanced stages (III–IV) when symptoms are already apparent. The NLST trial (2011): annual low-dose CT reduces lung cancer mortality by 20% and all-cause mortality by 6.7% — the largest benefit ever seen in cancer screening.
details: Why lung cancer is so hard to detect early: lungs have no pain receptors — early-stage lung tumors are completely asymptomatic. By the time coughing up blood, chest pain, or shortness of breath appear: the cancer is usually Stage III–IV. Five-year survival by stage: Stage IA (tumor < 3cm, not spread): 92%. Stage IIB: 53%. Stage IIIA: 36%. Stage IV (metastatic): 10%. This is why CT screening can save lives — detecting tumors at Stage IA when they can be completely removed.

Low-dose CT — how it works: low-dose CT (LDCT) uses 1.5 mSv of radiation (approximately half a chest X-ray, or 6 months of background radiation). The scan takes less than 5 minutes and requires no injection or contrast. Results are classified by Lung-RADS (1–4): Lung-RADS 1: no nodules — repeat annually. Lung-RADS 4X: highly suspicious — biopsy or further evaluation. Most detected "nodules" are benign (scar tissue, old infections) — requires experienced radiologist interpretation. Smoking cessation (if still smoking) remains the most important intervention.

NLST trial results and current evidence: the NLST (National Lung Screening Trial, US 2002–2004, 53,454 heavy smokers): annual LDCT vs. annual chest X-ray — LDCT reduced lung cancer mortality by 20% and all-cause mortality by 6.7%. Follow-up NELSON trial (Europe, 2020): LDCT vs. no screening — lung cancer mortality reduced 24% in men and 33% in women. These are the strongest evidence bases for LDCT screening. ACS, USPSTF, and major oncology societies now recommend annual LDCT for eligible high-risk individuals.

Eligibility criteria (USPSTF 2021): age 50–80 years AND currently smoking or quit within the past 15 years AND ≥ 20 pack-years of smoking history (pack-year = packs per day × years smoked). Example: smoking 1 pack/day for 20 years = 20 pack-years; or 2 packs/day for 10 years = 20 pack-years. Shared decision-making: discuss benefits, risks (false positives, unnecessary biopsies, radiation), and the critical importance of continued smoking cessation. Not recommended for non-smokers — benefit does not outweigh risk of false positives.

False positives — the main concern: approximately 20–30% of LDCT screens detect a pulmonary nodule, but > 95% of these are benign. This leads to: follow-up CTs to monitor the nodule (most common), PET scans, bronchoscopy, or — rarely — lung biopsy for indeterminate nodules. Risk of surgical complication from unnecessary biopsy: approximately 1–2%. The emotional toll of "suspicious" findings before they are confirmed benign is also significant. Experienced high-volume centers have lower false-positive rates.

Lung cancer in Vietnam: lung cancer is the most common cancer in Vietnamese men (~ 22% of male cancers) and a major cause of death. Over 85% of cases in Vietnam are attributed to smoking, though air pollution and occupational exposures also play a role. Lung cancer screening (LDCT) is not yet widely available in Vietnam — most cases are diagnosed late. Major oncology centers: Vietnam National Cancer Hospital (K Hospital), HCM City Oncology Hospital, Cho Ray Hospital. Smoking cessation should always be the first priority — it reduces lung cancer risk by 50% within 5 years of quitting.

points.label: Eligibility: ages 50–80 + ≥ 20 pack-years + current or recent smoker
points.note: Screening saves lives only in this high-risk group — not recommended for non-smokers

points.label: LDCT: 5-minute scan, no injection, radiation = half a chest X-ray
points.note: NLST: 20% reduction in lung cancer mortality, 6.7% reduction in all-cause mortality

sm_principles_tr.title: Consistency in Measurement Conditions
sm_principles_tr.subtitle: Same time · Same device · Same state
sm_principles_tr.keyFact: 🔄 Consistency matters more than frequency. Weighing yourself 10 times a week under different conditions each time is less valuable than weighing once a week under identical, standardized conditions. Measurement variability is the greatest enemy of health tracking — it creates "noise" that masks the true signal.
details: Why measurement conditions matter more than frequency: every health metric has natural "noise" due to physiology — body weight fluctuates by 1–2 kg per day due to water, glycogen, and food; blood pressure varies by 10–20 mmHg depending on time of day, stress, and recent activity. If you measure under different conditions each time, you are measuring noise rather than the true signal. Only when measurement conditions are controlled does the observed change reflect a real change in the body.

Standardizing each metric — specifically: Body weight: morning, after using the bathroom, before eating or drinking, same amount of clothing (or none), same scale. Blood pressure: sit quietly for 5 minutes before measuring, morning + evening, before taking medication (if applicable), no coffee or exercise for 30 minutes prior. Resting heart rate: immediately upon waking, before getting out of bed. Blood glucose: fasting (8 hours, in the morning) and exactly 2 hours after a meal. Waist circumference: morning, after a normal exhale, same position on the body, same measuring tape.

Equipment — choose and use consistently: every device has its own systematic error. If your scale always reads 0.5 kg higher than the true value — it does not matter, as long as you use the same scale every time (the trend remains accurate). The problem arises when you switch scales midway — then you cannot tell whether a change reflects your body or your equipment. For blood pressure: always use the same arm (the non-dominant arm typically reads 5–10 mmHg lower), with the cuff in the same position.

Measurement timing — circadian rhythm affects every metric: the body has a 24-hour biological rhythm that influences all physiological measures. Blood pressure is lowest at 3–4 AM, rises progressively and peaks in the morning (morning surge) — which is why strokes are more common in the morning. Cortisol is highest at 8–9 AM (affecting blood glucose and blood pressure). Body temperature is lowest at 4–6 AM and highest at 5–7 PM. If you measure blood pressure in the morning one day and the afternoon the next, the difference may be due to the time of day, not your health.

Creating a ritual (fixed habit): anchor measurements to an existing daily action (habit stacking). For example: "After using the bathroom, I step on the scale" — no need to remember, no reminder needed. "Before brewing morning coffee, I sit for 5 minutes and measure my blood pressure." This both ensures consistent timing and builds a sustainable habit. James Clear (Atomic Habits): the strongest habits are those anchored to an existing environment or behavior.

Recording abnormal conditions: when you must measure under unusual conditions (afternoon instead of morning, after exercise), record a note rather than discarding the data. That data point can still be useful — but it must be flagged so it is not confused with normal readings when analyzing trends. Apps such as Cronometer, Samsung Health, and Apple Health all allow notes to be added alongside each measurement.

points.label: Same conditions every time > frequent measurements under varying conditions
points.note: Noise hides the signal — controlling conditions reveals real change

sm_principles_tr.title: Record Immediately, Without Delay
sm_principles_tr.subtitle: Memory is unreliable · Record the moment you measure
sm_principles_tr.keyFact: ✍️ Human memory is not designed to store precise numbers. After 20 minutes, we forget 40% of what we just experienced (Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve). For health metrics — the number you recall hours later is usually a "feels about right" figure rather than the actual reading, distorted by current expectations and emotions.
details: Forgetting Curve (Hermann Ebbinghaus, 1885): the classic memory study — immediately after learning/observing = 100% retained. After 20 minutes = 60% retained. After 1 hour = 44% retained. After 1 day = 33% retained. After 1 week = 25% retained. With blood pressure or blood glucose readings — you will not accurately remember whether it was 127/84 or 132/86 after a few hours. You will remember "blood pressure was a bit high" — but exactly how high will no longer be certain.

Memory distortion — we do not just forget, we misremember: if you feel tired today, you tend to recall your blood pressure from yesterday as "higher than usual" even if it was actually normal. Confirmation bias: we remember numbers that align with our current beliefs or emotions. In health tracking, this is particularly dangerous — it can lead to unnecessary anxiety or cause you to overlook a real problem.

Record immediately — set up a specific process: place your phone next to the scale and blood pressure monitor — it is impossible to finish measuring without seeing the phone right there. Use apps that integrate via Bluetooth (Omron Connect, Withings Health Mate, Xiaomi Mi Fit) — data syncs automatically the moment you finish measuring, no manual entry needed. If you do not have a smart device: use a sticky note attached at the measurement location — write on it immediately, then transfer to an app or spreadsheet at the end of the day.

Minimal recording system — friction must be zero: the formula for success: every additional second added to the recording process reduces long-term compliance by approximately 10%. Best: Bluetooth device syncs automatically → nothing to do. Good: shortcut on the phone home screen that opens directly to the health app input screen. Avoid: "I will enter it into Excel after breakfast" — too many steps, too many opportunities to forget or postpone. Apple Health Shortcut: create a shortcut to enter weight or blood pressure with 1 tap from the lock screen.

Paper backup — when you do not have your phone: a small notebook or notepad placed next to the scale and blood pressure monitor is the best backup. Write the date, time, and reading. Benefits of paper: no need to unlock a phone, no notifications to distract you, no concern about battery. Research on note-taking: writing by hand improves retention compared to tapping on a phone — so even when using an app, the act of looking at and writing down a number by hand once helps you truly "see" the data rather than just tapping blindly.

Handling missed data: if you forget to record for a day — do not try to recall and fill in. Write "no data" or leave it blank — this is more honest. Gaps in data are not a problem — they are information (showing which days you tend to skip). If you miss several consecutive days — do not "compensate" by measuring multiple times in a single day. Instead, reset the habit: identify why you missed (traveling? busy?) and find a solution for next time.

sm_principles_tr.title: Look at 4–8 Week Trends
sm_principles_tr.subtitle: Ignore daily fluctuations · The signal lies in the trend
sm_principles_tr.keyFact: 📈 Every single data point is "noise" — the trend is the "signal." Weight increasing by 0.8 kg from yesterday to today means nothing — but weight increasing by 0.8 kg every week for 4 consecutive weeks is a clear signal. The human brain is not naturally good at spotting trends — we need tools to filter out noise.
details: Noise vs Signal — distinguishing two types of change: "Noise" (random variation): temporary, unrelated to actual health. Examples: weight up 1.5 kg after a salty dinner (water retention). Blood pressure up 15 mmHg after a stressful meeting. Heart rate up 8 bpm after 3 cups of coffee. "Signal" (true change): systematic, stable over time, reflecting a real underlying shift. Examples: weight increasing by 0.5 kg/week steadily for 8 weeks. Average blood pressure up 8 mmHg over 4 weeks. Resting heart rate down 7 bpm after 12 weeks of consistent running.

Time needed to see a clear trend: Body weight: 2–4 weeks (daily fluctuations mask shorter trends). Blood pressure: 7–14 days (7-day average gives a reliable reading). Resting heart rate: 4–8 weeks (cardiovascular adaptation is slow). Blood glucose (HbA1c): 8–12 weeks (reflects a 2–3 month average). Energy levels: 2–4 weeks (to recognize weekly patterns). Conclusion: for most metrics, you need at least 4 weeks of data to form a reliable picture.

Tools for calculating trend lines: Happy Scale app (iOS): automatically calculates a trend line from weight data, filtering out daily fluctuations — displays a weighted moving average. Apple Health: automatic charts with trend line. Google Sheets / Excel: AVERAGE(rolling window) function or =TREND(). Withings / Garmin / Oura: automatic dashboards with trend analysis. Whoop: strain vs recovery trends by week and month. Principle: any app that displays a trend line (not just individual data points) is better than looking at raw numbers.

Moving average — the simplest way to filter noise: 7-day moving average for weight: (day 1 + day 2 + day 3 + day 4 + day 5 + day 6 + day 7) / 7. How does today's value compare to last week's? If up 0.1–0.2 kg/week: mild upward trend. If down 0.2–0.5 kg/week: losing fat. Manual approach: calculate the average of the last 7 days each week and compare to the previous week — 5 minutes per week, no complex software needed.

Normal variability — no need to worry: Body weight: ±1.5 kg variation during the day — normal. Blood pressure: ±10 mmHg systolic between two readings 1 hour apart — normal. Heart rate: ±5–10 bpm day to day — normal. Blood glucose after eating: rises 40–60 mg/dL then returns to normal range within 2 hours — completely physiological. Abnormal variation (worth noting): blood pressure changing > 30 mmHg between two consecutive readings (5 minutes apart) without a clear reason. Weight up > 2 kg in a single day (unusual edema). Heart rate > 15 bpm above baseline lasting more than 2 days.

Periodic review — a schedule for looking back at data: Weekly (5 minutes on Sunday): look at the past 7 days — anything unusual? Monthly (15 minutes): compare 4 weeks — which direction is the trend heading? Quarterly (30 minutes): review 3 months — have goals been met? What adjustments are needed? Regular reviews transform raw data into actionable insights. No review = data has no value. Set a specific time (e.g., Sunday evening after dinner) and stick to it.

points.label: Need 4+ weeks of data to see a reliable trend
points.note: Less than 4 weeks: impossible to distinguish noise from true signal

sm_principles_tr.title: Do Not Obsess Over Numbers
sm_principles_tr.subtitle: Notice changes · Do not optimize every day
sm_principles_tr.keyFact: 🧘 Health tracking is a tool — not a goal. When tracking starts to cause anxiety, obsession, or negatively affects your behavior (eating less because your weight went up, refusing meals with friends, checking blood pressure 5 times a day), that is a sign to pause and reassess your relationship with your data.
details: The right purpose of health tracking: detect abnormal trends early so you can act in time. Understand how your body responds to lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, sleep). Have objective data to discuss with your doctor. Stay motivated by seeing clear progress. NOT: achieving a perfect score every day, comparing with others, optimizing every detail. If tracking does not help you live better, you do not need to do it.

Orthorexia Nervosa and "quantified self" obsession: Orthorexia Nervosa: an obsession with "perfect" eating — which can extend to an obsession with "perfect" health metrics. Quantified Self Obsession: an increasingly common phenomenon with wearables — users track everything, feel anxious when data is missing, and feel bad when numbers are not good. Research (Etkin, 2016): excessive tracking can reduce intrinsic motivation — you start exercising because of step counts rather than because it feels good.

Warning signs — when tracking is becoming unhealthy: weighing yourself more than once a day and feeling compelled to. Canceling plans to eat with friends or family out of concern about your metrics. Feeling guilty or like a failure when one day's numbers are "imperfect." Losing sleep over worry about a small abnormal reading. Constantly searching for the meaning of every minor change. Every lifestyle decision must be based on numbers rather than how you feel.

Establishing healthy boundaries: only measure as frequently as necessary (weight 1×/week, blood pressure morning + evening — no more). Do not check the app multiple times a day. Have occasional days or weeks where you take a complete break from tracking. Do not share personal health metrics on social media to "compete." Remember that the goal is to live well — not to have beautiful data. If one metric consistently causes anxiety, temporarily stop tracking that metric for 2–4 weeks.

"Good enough" standards rather than "perfect": body weight within ±2 kg of target = good, no need for constant adjustment. Weekly average blood pressure < 130/80 mmHg = good, no further optimization needed. Sleep of 7+ hours for 5 out of 7 nights per week = good, no need for exactly 8 hours every single night. Resting heart rate stable or gradually declining over months = good. The 80/20 principle: if you achieve the "good" level 80% of days, your long-term health outcomes will be good — you do not need 100% every day.

When to stop or reduce tracking: if tracking causes more stress than benefit, try: stopping completely for 2 weeks and observing how you feel. If you feel relieved — you may have been tracking too much, and need to find a better balance. If you feel anxious without data — this is also a signal worth paying attention to (data dependency). Consult a mental health professional if health anxiety (excessive worry about health) is affecting your daily life. Your doctor needs trends — not every data point.

points.note: Tracking is a tool that serves health — not a goal in itself

Record fasting blood glucose after 8 hours of no food; if possible, test 2 hours post-meal as well to understand your glycemic response pattern.
Get a lipid panel (Total-C, LDL, HDL, Triglycerides) — this snapshot cannot be recreated retroactively and serves as your starting benchmark for months ahead.
Weigh yourself at the same time each day (morning, after bathroom) for 7 days; average the readings to eliminate daily fluid fluctuation noise.
Document your lifestyle: sleep hours, daily step count, weekly exercise frequency, and dietary patterns — these contextualise your biomarkers.
Set 2–3 specific, measurable health goals (e.g., 'reduce SBP by 10 mmHg in 12 weeks') and write them down — written goals have a measurably higher completion rate than mental intentions.

Track your nutrition using a simple plate method: half plate vegetables, quarter protein, quarter complex carbs — no calorie counting required for this phase, just consistent structure.
Aim for 7,000–10,000 steps daily; a cheap pedometer or phone step counter is sufficient. Walking after meals has proven effects on post-meal blood glucose control.
Log sleep duration and quality each morning with a 1–5 score — chronic sleep under 6 hours elevates cortisol, which directly raises blood pressure and disrupts glucose regulation.
Weigh in weekly (not daily in this phase) to track trend rather than fluctuation — a downward or stable trend over 4 weeks is the signal that matters.
Review your Week 1–2 baseline at the end of Week 6 to calculate preliminary progress and adjust any single habit that is proving unsustainable.

rm_phases_tr.keyFact: WHO estimates that 80% of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and many cancers are preventable through lifestyle alone. Weeks 7–10 move from passive tracking to active intervention — adjusting diet, exercise intensity, and stress management based on your 6-week data.

Reduce sodium intake to under 2,000 mg/day (WHO) or 1,500 mg/day (AHA for high BP) — processed foods, restaurant meals, and condiments are the primary hidden sources.
Add evidence-based dietary tweaks: increase omega-3-rich fish (2 servings/week), reduce saturated fat to under 7% of calories, and replace refined carbs with whole grains.
Begin a simple stress protocol: 5–10 minutes of diaphragmatic breathing or guided meditation daily — chronic stress is an independent cardiovascular risk factor.
Schedule a mid-roadmap health check (repeat key biomarkers) to quantify Phase 1→3 improvements and motivate continued adherence through visible data.

Set a 6-month and 12-month health review calendar reminder now; annual check-ups without personal tracking data miss most early warning signs.
Build social accountability: share your weekly health summary with one trusted person (partner, friend, or online community) — social commitment increases long-term adherence significantly.
Create your personalised emergency protocol: know your trigger thresholds (e.g., BP > 140/90, fasting glucose > 7.0 mmol/L) and the exact action steps for each scenario.
Celebrate measurable wins explicitly — write them down, share them — positive reinforcement is the neurological mechanism that converts short-term behaviour into long-term identity.

sm_metrics_tr.label: Energy Level
sm_metrics_tr.note: Track with numbers or emojis. Helps identify patterns related to diet, sleep, and activity.
sm_metrics_tr.keyFact: Consistent low energy is a sign worth investigating with a doctor
details: Rate your energy on a 1–10 scale at mid-morning (around 10 am) and mid-afternoon (around 3 pm).
Over 2–4 weeks, patterns emerge linking energy to meals, sleep quality, hydration, and exercise.
Low energy after lunch (post-meal dip) is normal; severe crashes warrant dietary review.
Chronically low energy (< 5 most days) may indicate nutritional deficiency, thyroid issues, or burnout.
Tracking emojis (😴😐😊⚡) is equally valid — choose whichever you will consistently maintain.

pillarF.title: Công Cụ & Tài Nguyên
pillarF.subtitle: Công Cụ
pillarF.description: Checklist, mẫu và bộ test để theo dõi hành trình sống khỏe.

sections.title: Checklist Hàng Ngày
items: 10–20 phút vận động (tập, đi bộ, giãn cơ)
2 nắm rau/bữa — rau xanh, củ quả tươi
1 nguồn đạm/bữa chính — thịt, cá, trứng, đậu hũ
Uống đủ 1.5–2 lít nước
Ngủ đủ 7–8 tiếng, đi ngủ trước 23h
5 phút thở hoặc thiền — bất kỳ lúc nào
Tránh điện thoại 30 phút trước khi ngủ

sections.title: Checklist Hàng Tuần
items: Hoàn thành 3–5 buổi tập như đã lên kế hoạch
Chuẩn bị bữa ăn sẵn 1–2h cuối tuần
Kiểm tra tiến bộ: cân nặng, vòng eo, cảm giác chung
Lên lịch tập tuần tới — xác nhận ngày/giờ cụ thể
Dành 1h cho hoạt động thư giãn yêu thích (đọc sách, đi dạo)

sections.title: Mẫu Theo Dõi
items: Nhật ký tập luyện: ngày · bài tập · hiệp · lần · cảm giác
Mẫu lên thực đơn 7 ngày: sáng/trưa/tối + ăn vặt
Thói quen buổi sáng 15 phút: nước · ánh sáng · vận động · thiền
Thói quen buổi tối 20 phút: tắm · đọc/ghi chép · không điện thoại

sections.title: Bộ Test Tiến Bộ 4 Tuần
items: Test sức bền: đi bộ nhanh 6 phút — đo quãng đường
Test sức mạnh: số lần chống đẩy tối đa + gập chân tối đa
Test linh hoạt: chạm ngón tay sàn khi đứng thẳng
Đo vòng eo, cân nặng vào sáng sớm (trước ăn)
Ghi lại kết quả và so sánh sau 4 tuần, 8 tuần, 12 tuần

sections.title: Nhật Ký Buổi Tập (5 Câu Hỏi Sau Mỗi Buổi)
items: 1. Hôm nay tập bài gì? (liệt kê ngắn gọn)
2. Bao nhiêu phút?
3. Cảm giác cường độ 1–10?
4. Có đau bất thường nào không?
5. Lần sau tăng số lần, tăng số hiệp, tăng độ khó, hay duy trì?

checklist_items: Không điện thoại 30 phút trước ngủ
